title: Enovix Announces Design Win for Next-Generation Smart Eyewear - Curved Trapezoid Si-C Cell Showcasing Custom Form Factor Capabilities - Batteries News
content:
Enovix Announces Design Win for Next-Generation Smart Eyewear – Curved Trapezoid Si-C Cell Showcasing Custom Form Factor Capabilities
Leading Global Technology Company Funds Development of Custom Cell for New Wearable
Curved Trapezoid Si-C Cell Showcasing Custom Form Factor Capabilities
Production Expected to Begin in Q3 2027; Device Targeted for Q4 2027 Launch
FREMONT, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Enovix Corporation (“Enovix” or the “Company,” Nasdaq: ENVX), a leader in advanced silicon and silicon-carbon (Si-C) blend anode lithium-ion battery technology, today announced a design win with a leading global technology company, which has issued a purchase order for Non-Recurring Engineering (NRE) services for the development of a custom battery cell to power an upcoming smart eyewear product. Production is expected to begin in Q3 2027, and the device is currently targeted to reach the market in Q4 2027. The NRE order does not cover production volumes, which would be subject to a separate purchase order.
The cell is a curved trapezoid design with an anode containing Si-C, engineered for the customer’s product. Its shape is tailored to the device’s design requirements and demonstrates Enovix’s ability to deliver cells in form factors that the Company believes are difficult to produce with conventional manufacturing approaches.
Designed Around the Device, Not the Other Way Around
In wearables, the battery is often the component that dictates the product’s size, shape, and weight. Conventional cells come in a limited set of standard formats, which can force designers to compromise industrial design, comfort, or run time.
Enovix takes a different approach that gives device designers more creative freedom. Its architecture and manufacturing process enable custom battery dimensions and form factors, including curved and non-rectangular geometries, tailored to a product’s electronics. The result: a battery built around the product, opening new possibilities for wearable design.
For wearables, this flexibility can deliver tangible benefits:
Better fit and comfort.
Cells shaped to follow the contours of a device help create slimmer, lighter products that sit more naturally on the body throughout the day.
Longer run time.
Making full use of available internal space, combined with Enovix’s high-energy-density Si-C blend anode technology, can allow more energy to be packed into a small volume, which can extend time between charges.
Small, lightweight form factors.
Higher energy density per unit of volume and weight can let designers shrink the battery footprint or add capability without making the device bulkier.
Steven Bakos,
Chief Revenue Officer and General Manager of Enovix, said,
In wearables, every fraction of a millimeter and every gram matters.
”Battery design directly affects how a product looks, feels, and performs. There is growing demand for batteries that give product teams more room to innovate, and this program brings that opportunity to life. With a curved trapezoid cell and a Si-C anode, we’re helping the customer make the most of limited space while pursuing a distinctive design. It’s an example of how high energy density and custom form factors can support bolder ideas in smart eyewear and other wearables designed to fit naturally into people’s everyday lives.”
This program marks a step in Enovix’s efforts to expand its presence in wearable consumer electronics and aligns with the Company’s focus on markets where its battery technology addresses clear customer needs. Through customer-specific development work, Enovix aims to translate its battery technology into commercial opportunities across a range of applications.

title: New graphite paves way for rapid EV charging - Batteries News
content:
New graphite paves way for rapid EV charging
Lithium-ion batteries, like those found in cars, cell phones and cameras, often have anodes made of graphite. During charging, lithium ions move into the graphite anode. How quickly they can move through the graphite is one of the key factors limiting how fast a battery can charge.
James Tour
’s lab at Rice University has recently developed a new kind of synthetic graphite, one that supports much faster charging and can be produced in a fraction of a second.
Tour, the
T.T. and W.F. Chao
Professor of Chemistry and corresponding author on this study, said:
This method could help make future electric vehicle batteries charge faster while reducing the cost and environmental impact of battery manufacturing,
“Our analysis suggests it could reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions by more than 80% compared with conventional graphite production.”
The study, recently published in
Advanced Materials
, describes a method that uses a small amount of a nickel compound and an extremely short, powerful electrical pulse. The nickel compound is added to petroleum coke, a low-cost carbon residue from oil refining. A single electrical pulse then briefly heats the mixture to about 2,500 C, triggering its rapid transformation into graphite — the same form of carbon found in pencil leads. But in this case, the process produces highly ordered, low-defect graphite with promising properties for fast-charging battery anodes.
Graphite is a two-dimensional material, meaning that it is created from layers of horizontal structures only one atom thick stacked on top of each other. In graphite, each layer is comprised of carbon atoms neatly ordered into hexagons. When the research team added a little bit of nickel compound to the petroleum coke, the carbon atoms were able to quickly organize around the tiny nickel particles.
Haojie Zhu
, postdoctoral associate and first author of the paper, said:
The nickel acts almost like a temporary construction worker, helping the carbon atoms organize themselves into a highly ordered, layered graphite structure,
“Usually, creating graphite requires prolonged heating at extremely high temperatures for long periods, but this method allows us to do it in just two-tenths of a second.”
The nickel slightly expanded the interlayer spacing in the graphite, providing greater access for subsequent lithium entry during charging. When the team tested this nickel-formed graphite on a lithium-ion battery, they found it significantly outperformed conventional graphite for charging, tolerating a rate equivalent to a four-minute charging time. And it retained 80% of its capacity after 1,000 charge and discharge cycles, where the battery was fully drained and then charged up again.
This method addresses two major challenges simultaneously: improving battery fast-charging performance and simplifying the production of a key battery material,
“Imagine charging your battery in four minutes.”
The team found that the benefits of nickel-assisted graphite production remained even after more than 99% of the residual nickel was removed. This suggests that the main advantage comes from how nickel helps build the graphite structure rather than simply from nickel remaining in the material.
Surprisingly, more heat did not necessarily mean better graphite: At excessively high temperatures, much of the nickel was lost, while lower temperatures resulted in less ordered graphite.
We identified the Goldilocks region for graphite preparation,
What I find especially exciting is that a process lasting just 0.2 seconds can produce graphite with such impressive fast-charging performance,
“Making better materials is not always about using more energy or processing them for longer but about applying the right conditions at exactly the right moment.”
This work was funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (FA9550-22-1-0526), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, ERDC (W912HZ-21-2-0050, W912HZ-24-2-0027), the Department of Energy NERSC award (BES-ERCAP0027822, B.I.Y.) and the Welch Foundation (C-2065).

UK – Car battery gigafactory builder drops out
The company building the UK’s biggest electric vehicle (EV) battery factory has said its opening remains “on track”, despite a major contractor stepping away from the project for the second time in six months.
The gigafactory near Bridgwater in Somerset, is being led by Agratas and built
on the site of a former ordinance factory
, creating around 4,600 jobs once open.
Contractor TSL, which is building the factory’s exterior,
will step down
once that work is complete, but the company has declined to say why and it is unclear if it had planned further involvement.
Buckinghamshire-based TSL only joined the project in June after previous lead contractor Sir Robert McAlpine
ended its involvement
Agratas, part of the Tata Group which owns Jaguar Land Rover, said it will not need to replace TSL as it is already working with another contractor – NG Bailey – who will carry out the remaining work fitting out the inside of the factory.
A spokesperson for Agratas
We are on track to meet our customer requirements.
“The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility’s launch phase.”
Construction of the factory on the 616 acre (249.2 hectare) brownfield location near Bridgwater was expected to take two years, with about 2,000 people working on site this year.
Project leader Agratas said in the summer the original 2026 factory opening date had been pushed back to 2027, and has now confirmed it will be the end of that year.
The company said 1,500 operational jobs would be created in 2027, with 4,600 jobs on offer once it expands across the whole site.

title: Netherlands - Exploration of criteria for safe and sustainable home battery systems - Batteries News
content:
Netherlands – Exploration of criteria for safe and sustainable home battery systems
More and more households are installing home batteries to store the energy they generate themselves. While this new development can contribute to the energy transition, the production of home battery systems also uses energy and scarce raw materials. Additionally, substances used in home batteries can be harmful to the environment. RIVM has explored assessment criteria for an ‘ideal’ home battery system. For example, safety, sustainability, circularity of materials and cybersecurity. Regarding sustainability and circularity in particular, further research is needed to determine to what extent home batteries meet these criteria.
RIVM based its explorations on the
Safe and Sustainable by Design
framework. By applying the principles of this framework, developers and policy makers can already take safety and sustainability throughout a battery’s lifecycle into account in the design phase.
Greater focus required on safely and sustainably designed home battery systems
RIVM investigated the necessary criteria for and properties of an ‘ideal’ home battery. These criteria related to the areas of functionality, safety of substances, physical safety, use of critical resources, circularity of materials, sustainability and cybersecurity.
RIVM compared this ‘ideal’ home battery to home battery systems currently available or expected on the market in the coming years.
Example of promising developments
Different types of home battery systems have very different environmental impacts. For example, one of the lithium-ion batteries examined contains high amounts of harmful and scarce substances. There are also home batteries under development that are safer and potentially more sustainable, such as natrium-ion batteries. These contain barely any harmful substances and have a lower risk of fire due to overheating.
Next step: Development of criteria into actionable requirements
This exploratory research identifies opportunities for the development of safe, sustainable home battery systems, as well as the knowledge that is needed  to enable this. RIVM recommends research into data on the sustainability and circularity of home battery systems and the translation of criteria into actionable requirements. That knowledge would support more focus on these aspects in the development of home battery systems, government incentives and the purchase and installation of such systems.
This exploratory research by RIVM was funded by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy.

title: Indonesian supply constraints and shifting battery chemistry reshape global nickel and cobalt markets - Batteries News
content:
Indonesian supply constraints and shifting battery chemistry reshape global nickel and cobalt markets
Class II nickel tightness developing as Indonesian NPI output falls in 2026
Sulphur supply shock puts over 600 kt Ni of incoming MHP capacity at risk
Global refined cobalt consumption forecast to contract in 2026
Structural shifts are reshaping the global nickel and cobalt markets, as Indonesian supply disruptions, declining ore grades, and accelerating battery chemistry transitions converge, according to new research from Wood Mackenzie.
The report, “Takeaways from 2026 Antaike Nickel and Cobalt Conference”, identifies five themes that are fundamentally reconfiguring supply and demand dynamics across both markets.
Indonesia faces a confluence of supply headwinds
Indonesian supply disruption in 2026 reflects three concurrent pressures: tighter mining quota restrictions, a severe sulphur supply shock, and El Nino-related drought.
Prior to the Middle East conflict, approximately 80% of Indonesia’s sulphur imports originated from the region. The subsequent Strait of Hormuz closure triggered a 29% year-on-year decline in total sulphur imports in H1 2026, with average prices nearly tripling. More than 600 kt Ni of incoming MHP project capacity has been identified as potentially at risk.
Ziyi Liu,
research associate at Wood Mackenzie, noted:
Sulphur supply constraints are unlikely to ease quickly,
“Logistics normalisation takes time even if conflict-related disruptions subside, and persistent competition from the fertiliser sector limits the reallocation of available supply to industrial buyers.”
Drought conditions have added a further layer of disruption, with smelters at IMIP reporting production cuts of 30 to 45% in late September due to disrupted coal-barging routes and acute water shortages across Central and South Sulawesi.
A structural Class II tightness is developing
Declining saprolite ore grades in Indonesia are driving a meaningful contraction in nickel pig iron (NPI) output in 2026, reversing several years of consistent growth. Stainless steel mills have responded by sharply increasing their consumption of pure nickel as a substitute, with scrap ratios rising from approximately 21–22% a few years ago to around 25% in 2026.
Class II market tightness is expected to persist through the medium term if Indonesian output does not recover materially,
“The pace of recovery will depend on how quickly NPI production rebounds, whether scrap availability can partially offset the gap, and how far stainless mills are willing to absorb the higher input cost of primary metal.”
Stainless steel demand resilient but reconfiguring
Stainless steel melt output continued to grow in 2026, though production gains have outpaced real end-use demand. Chinese net stainless exports contracted year on year as the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism entered its definitive phase, and Indonesian export volumes softened under anti-dumping measures.
Mills are shifting toward higher-value corrosion-resistant and alloy grades as commodity stainless margins compress. However, Wood Mackenzie cautions that capacity growth in special alloy grades risks running ahead of specialised end-use demand, and that non-battery channels alone are insufficient to absorb the structural Class I surplus without a concurrent supply-side adjustment.
Battery recycling enters its formative phase
Battery recycling remains a growing but still modest component of nickel and cobalt supply, with the large-scale retirement wave from first-generation EV batteries expected to ramp up materially after 2030. Early commercial differentiation is nonetheless emerging, with European and North American buyers placing increasing value on battery materials with verifiable, low-carbon supply chains.
If the carbon footprint premium becomes a durable feature of the market, it will create a structural incentive for investment in traceable recycling capacity well before volumes reach a scale that challenges primary supply economics,

title: Dynamic battery reserves can deliver network benefits - Batteries News
content:
Dynamic battery reserves can deliver network benefits
Transmission lines are often run well below capacity so the network can cope if a fault occurs. This increasingly limits renewable energy flows.
Single batteries already help transmission lines carry more power. The Victorian Big Battery and Waratah Super Battery do this under SIPS contracts, with the Waratah contract now more flexible to improve utilisation.
A Flexible BESS–SIPS Portfolio could extend this service so that multiple batteries could be enabled to support transmission lines to run at higher levels, unlocking more renewable energy from REZs.
The concept should be tested through modelling and a trial, and optimal procurement routes identified. A new System Operator function should be established to co-ordinate the Flexible BESS–SIPS Portfolio.

title: IVECO BUS unveils next-generation batteries delivering greater range and warranty option of up to 15 years - Batteries News

IVECO BUS unveils next-generation batteries delivering greater range and warranty option of up to 15 years
IVECO BUS boosts the performance of its electric range with a new generation of NMC batteries for its electric city and intercity buses, delivering up to 100 km of additional driving range and offering the option of extending battery warranty coverage to 15 years. First deliveries are scheduled for the second quarter of 2027.
Boosted performance for electric city and intercity buses
IVECO BUS introduces a new generation of NMC batteries across all heavy-duty E‑WAY and CROSSWAY ELEC models, including the Low Entry version. Within the same footprint, the new batteries offer approximately 15% higher energy density than the previous generation and deliver up to 100 km of additional range, depending on the model and configuration. Operators also have the option of extending the battery warranty coverage to up to 15 years.
Battery pack capacity rises to 80 kWh
This new generation of batteries is based on the NMC (nickel, manganese, cobalt) technology already used in the brand’s electric vehicles. Thanks to an optimised design and improved modules, capacity per battery pack has increased to 80 kWh, compared with 69 kWh for the previous generation. For operators, this development offers greater flexibility to tailor each vehicle’s configuration more precisely to its operational requirements.
Modular battery configurations tailored to operational needs
The E-WAY city bus models offer configurations ranging from 4 to 9 battery packs, providing total capacities of 320 to 720 kWh, depending on the version: midibus, standard or articulated. On 12-metre versions, the new generation of batteries delivers up to 100 km of additional range.
The CROSSWAY Low Entry ELEC offers 4 to 7 battery packs, delivering a total capacity of 320 to 560 kWh and up to 100 km of additional range. The CROSSWAY ELEC is available with 3 to 6 battery packs, providing a total capacity of 240 to 480 kWh.
This modular approach enables customers to match energy capacity precisely to their routes and distances travelled, investing only in the energy they actually need.
Extended warranty coverage enhances operating cost predictability
The option of extending the battery warranty to 15 years gives operators better long-term visibility over vehicle operating costs, helping them manage their total cost of ownership (TCO).
In practice, this new generation of batteries enables operators to tailor their investment to the requirements of each mission: depending on operational needs, the same driving range can be achieved with one fewer battery pack, also allowing for increased passenger capacity. Combined with the elimination of mid-life battery replacement, this reduction in the number of packs can deliver savings of up to 17% on the GX 337 ELEC’s total cost of ownership over 15 years of operation.
Enhanced safety, even in standby mode
Already compliant with UNECE R100.4, the batteries also incorporate additional safety features designed to further enhance system reliability. If thermal runaway is detected, even in standby mode, the battery triggers an alert. In addition to this warning function, each module is equipped with a fire extinguisher that releases an extinguishing agent in the event of a fire.
First deliveries scheduled for Q2 2027
The first deliveries are scheduled for the second quarter of 2027. By offering greater flexibility in battery configuration, the new generation enables operators to balance driving range, passenger capacity, and total cost of ownership according to each route’s specific operational requirements.
IVECO BUS, a brand of Iveco Group N.V. (EXM: IVG), develops, manufactures and markets a full range of passenger transport vehicles tailored to a broad spectrum of mobility applications, including urban, intercity, school, scheduled line and tourism operations.
With an international presence, IVECO BUS supports private transport operators and public transport authorities in their energy transition through a technology-neutral approach encompassing biofuels, biomethane, battery-electric and fuel cell technologies.
Through an extensive service network, IVECO BUS supports customers wherever its vehicles are deployed.
In addition, through its
Energy Mobility Solutions
offering, IVECO BUS provides tailored support for the planning and deployment of complex electrification projects.
A wide range of IVECO ON connected services, developed to optimise the operation and maintenance of fleets operating with different energy technologies, completes IVECO BUS’s comprehensive offering.
The company employs over 6,550 people and operates seven manufacturing plants in Europe and Latin America: Annonay and Rorthais in France, Vysoké Myto in the Czech Republic, Brescia and Foggia in Italy, Sete Lagoas in Brazil, and Córdoba in Argentina.

title: Siemens launches world's first heavy duty direct current contactor for up to 1500 V - Batteries News
content:
Siemens launches world’s first heavy duty direct current contactor for up to 1500 V
Innovative hybrid technology combines semiconductors and mechanics
Wear-free electronic switching of up to 1,500 V and 600 A
Complements Siemens’ comprehensive direct current portfolio
Ideal for switching in energy storage, e-mobility charging, PV and marine applications
Siemens is expanding its direct current (DC) portfolio with the world’s first semiconductor-based heavy duty DC contactor for high DC currents up to 600 A and voltages up to 1,500 V. The new SIRIUS 3QC1 contactor enables galvanic isolation, and reliable and wear-free switching of high DC loads through innovative semiconductor technology. The enlarged portfolio allows customers to more quickly adopt DC grids.
DC systems offer significant advantages, including up to 8 percent energy savings by reducing AC-DC conversions and enabling direct renewable energy and battery storage integration. They can also save up to 50 percent on materials due to reduced cross-section of cables and the need for fewer conductors and components.
The heavy duty DC contactor combines the advantages of semiconductors and mechanical contacts: the semiconductors handle the actual switching process precisely and wear-free, preventing any arcing. During operation, the mechanical contacts are closed and ensure low-loss current conduction. This combination leads to exceptional durability of at least 150,000 switching cycles. The mechanical contacts also ensure galvanic isolation for maximum reliable interruption of the conducting path.
Markus Grabmeier,
President Electrical Products at Siemens AG, said:
The shift to direct current is a gamechanger for energy efficiency and the integration of renewables.
”Our new DC contactor is a crucial building block in this transformation, making sustainable power practical and scalable. It’s a prime example of how Siemens’ innovations are accelerating the energy transition and paving the way for a more decarbonized world,”
A key feature of the SIRIUS 3QC1 is its bidirectionality, which allows it to switch independently of the current’s direction. This makes it the ideal solution for applications involving charging and discharging processes, such as battery energy storage systems (BESS). These BESS facilities can utilize heavy duty DC contactors in standard power racks (100 kW) and high-power racks (up to 375 kW / 300 A at 1,500 V). In e-mobility, they support megawatt fast-charging stations for fleets, e-trucks, and e-buses, with power ratings up to 1,000 kW. The technology is also suitable for marine applications, specifically on ships. Furthermore, it can be used in industrial DC microgrids to couple PV and storage, thereby maximizing independence from AC grid failures.
With the SIRIUS 3QC1 contactor, Siemens offers a simple, cost-effective, compact and familiar design featuring a contactor and a fuse. This solution provides low initial investment costs, and due to the robustness achieved through wear-free switching, the device is durable and maintenance-free, thereby reducing the plant’s maintenance costs. The DC contactor is also remotely switchable, increasing operational convenience and eliminating the need for manual on-site intervention.
The SIRIUS 3QC1 heavy duty DC contactor will be available in several current ratings: 300 A, 400 A, 500 A, and 600 A. It will operate with a control voltage of 24 V DC and can function at extreme temperatures, from -25 °C to +60 °C, with up to 95 percent humidity. Its compact design includes an integrated display with status and condition LEDs.
The new heavy duty DC contactor will be presented to the public for the first time at the Smart Production Solutions (SPS) trade fair held from November 24 to 26, 2026 in Nuremberg, Germany. The Siemens booth will be in Hall 11.

title: Hyundai's new Mercury EV Concept will launch as the IONIQ M in 2027 [Images]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 27 2026 - 7:11 am PT
unveiled the Mercury Concept, a preview of its upcoming entry-level electric SUV set to launch as the IONIQ M in 2027.
Meet the Hyundai Mercury EV Concept
Following
the IONIQ V,
which went on sale in September, Hyundai offered a look at its upcoming IONIQ lineup for China at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27.
Hyundai’s Mercury Concept stole the spotlight. The concept previews its upcoming “B-segment premium smart SUV,” set to launch in China in 2027.
According to Hyundai, the IONIQ M will be “the most accessible entry-level model in the IONIQ universe.” Unfortunately, it’s designed specifically for China.
Like the IONIQ V, the electric SUV was developed by Hyundai Motor’s Chinese design and engineering team. As such, it features a unique style and advanced tech you won’t find in Hyundai’s vehicles sold in the US, Europe, or other overseas markets.
The SUV’s futuristic low-slung design is inspired by Mercury’s orbit around the sun. Up front, the shark-nose design and slim, edgy lights form Hyundai’s “H” badge, while an integrated rear spoiler adds to the compact, sporty look.
Hyundai said the production version will feature Zhuoyu L2++ ADAS and a high-tech cabin powered by ByteDance’s Doubao AI model.
A battery-swap version is also set to launch through Hyundai’s partnership with China’s CATL following the production IONIQ M.
The IONIQ M joins Hyundai’s EV lineup in 2027
The Mercury follows the Venus, now on sale as the IONIQ V, and the larger Earth SUV, as Hyundai’s third IONIQ Planet name designed for China. It will go on sale in 2027 as the IONIQ M, alongside the IONIQ V EREV.
In 2028, Hyundai will launch the production version of the Earth SUV, while two new energy vehicles will join the lineup in 2029.
While Hyundai didn’t reveal battery or powertrain specs, it will likely feature a similar setup to the IONIQ V.
Hyundai IONIQ V
is available in China with two CATL lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs: A 53.5 kWh battery paired with a 140 kW (188 hp) rear electric motor that offers a CLTC range of up to 540 km, or a 66.8 kWh battery paired with a 168 kW (225 hp) motor with a CLTC range of up to 650 km (404 miles).
Hyundai said the IONIQ M will be “the most accessible entry-level model in the IONIQ universe.” Given the IONIQ V starts at 109,900 yuan ($16,500), the production IONIQ M could be priced around 99,000 yuan ($15,000) in China.

title: This might be the real reason Elon Musk says Tesla's AI5 chip is going to Optimus
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Tesla Optimus
Fred Lambert
| Nov 27 2026 - 6:48 am PT
Elon Musk says Tesla’s cars don’t need the next-generation AI5 chip, so it’s going to Optimus first. A new report from Taiwan’s chip supply chain gives a more practical reason: Tesla won’t have enough AI5 chips for its cars until 2028.
According to
Commercial Times
, Tesla’s chip design partner Global Unichip (GUC) is giving its limited TSMC 3nm capacity for 2027 to Google and Microsoft data center chips first. That leaves Tesla with a relatively small AI5 allocation.
Musk: “Cars will remain at AI4”
Last Sunday, a Tesla owner asked Musk when AI5 would be in new cars. His answer: “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”
As we reported this week,
FSD v15 is basically AI4’s last shot
. Tesla engineers are already squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of the chip, and the AI4.5 refresh is mostly a move to LPDDR5X memory. Musk said Tesla cut AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB of RAM because “RAM is super expensive,” and that AI4 itself now costs twice as much due to memory and storage price hikes.
It’s quite a change in plans. In June 2024, Musk said AI5 would be in vehicles in the second half of 2025.
Tesla only taped out AI5 in April
, and Musk had already started describing its focus as Optimus and Tesla’s supercomputer clusters.
Google and Microsoft get the 3nm wafers first
The Commercial Times report, published today, describes GUC as the custom ASIC design partner on Tesla’s AI5 project. GUC is the design services house whose largest shareholder is TSMC, and it works mostly on data center silicon.
Industry sources told the paper that GUC’s 2027 allocation of TSMC’s N3 capacity is much larger than this year’s. But with AI compute demand exploding, it still can’t serve every big customer at once.
So GUC is prioritizing North American cloud projects, including Google’s Axion 2 and Axion 3 server processors and Microsoft’s in-house chips. Those orders carry high margins and good visibility. Tesla’s robot and car chip doesn’t make the front of the line.
The result, according to the report, is that Tesla’s initial 2027 wafer quota can’t support annual shipments for a fleet of millions of cars. The supply chain expects that limited AI5 volume to go first to Optimus, which needs a lot of compute but ships in small numbers, and only expects large-scale adoption in cars after N3 capacity expands further in 2028.
TSMC is adding 3nm capacity, but not fast. Its new 3nm fab in Tainan is scheduled for volume production in the first half of 2027, and its second Arizona fab, which Musk has said will produce AI5, in the second half of 2027.
Samsung doesn’t fix 2027 either
Tesla does have a second source.
Samsung is building its own version of AI5 on 2nm at its Taylor, Texas fab
, but it expects volume production of Tesla’s AI chips there in the second half of 2027.
Now look at the numbers. Tesla delivered roughly 1.6 million vehicles last year. Every one of them needs a self-driving computer.
Optimus is a different story. Tesla now plans to put AI5 in Optimus around April 2027 and
push external Optimus deliveries to late 2027
. Even an aggressive robot ramp next year is measured in thousands of units, not millions.
If your 2027 AI5 supply is a fraction of what a car program needs, Optimus is the only product Tesla has that can absorb it.
Electrek’s Take
Musk’s version is that cars don’t need AI5 because AI4 is “enough to solve superhuman driving.” The supply chain’s version is that Tesla can’t get enough AI5 chips to put in cars anyway. Both can be true at the same time, but only one of them explains the timing.
Look at how Tesla has been handling silicon this fall. It cut AI4.5 RAM. It cut AI5 RAM from 144GB to 72GB, then bumped it to 96GB a day later. It says AI4 costs double what it used to. That’s a company rationing chips and memory, not one choosing to leave a 12x compute upgrade on the shelf because it isn’t needed.
And if AI4 really were plenty, Tesla engineers wouldn’t be talking about squeezing out the last few percent of the chip for v15.
So here’s how we read it. Tesla had to pick where its scarce AI5 chips go in 2027, and it picked the low-volume product. “AI4 is enough” is the story that makes that decision sound like a choice. And it’s a story we heard about HW3, Tesla’s previous self-driving computer.

title: Congress just passed a major e-bike safety law. Here’s what it actually means
政策分类路径: 政策 > 监管落实型政策 > 信息不对称 > 安全与互联互通标准
政策分类依据: 美国立法要求CPSC将UL锂电池安全标准转为强制性联邦消费品安全标准
content:
Micah Toll
| Nov 27 2026 - 3:24 am PT
E-bike battery safety standards that have largely been voluntary across the US are on the verge of becoming mandatory federal requirements, following the passage of a major piece of legislation in Congress.
The US Senate unanimously passed
H.R. 973
, known as the Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act, on November 19. The House previously passed the bill in April 2025 by a 365-42 vote. The legislation now heads to the president for a signature.
So what does that actually mean for e-bikes and their batteries?
The biggest change is that the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) would be required to turn three widely used UL safety standards into mandatory federal consumer product safety standards. Those include UL 2271 for light electric vehicle batteries, UL 2849 for e-bike electrical systems, and UL 2272 for personal e-mobility devices such as electric scooters.
Currently, those standards are generally voluntary at the federal level, though some jurisdictions have already made them mandatory. New York City, for example, r
equires certification to applicable UL standards
for e-bikes, batteries, and other micromobility devices sold in the city.
If H.R. 973 becomes law, that approach would effectively go nationwide.
The bill gives the CPSC 180 days after enactment to promulgate the three standards as final consumer product safety standards. And this isn’t simply a one-time requirement based on today’s standards. Future revisions would generally become federal requirements 180 days after the CPSC is notified, unless the agency determines that a revision doesn’t improve safety.
What does this mean for the e-bike industry?
For established e-bike companies already selling UL-certified products, the immediate impact may be relatively small. Many major brands have already moved toward UL 2849 certification, particularly as retailers and municipalities have increasingly demanded it.
The bigger impact is likely to be felt at the lower end of the market, where inexpensive e-bikes, replacement batteries, and direct-import products have continued to enter the US without certification to recognized safety standards.
Importantly, UL certification isn’t a guarantee that a lithium-ion battery can never catch fire. Damage, improper repairs, incompatible chargers, manufacturing defects, and other problems can still create hazards.
But the standards are designed to test batteries and electrical systems against foreseeable electrical, mechanical, and environmental stresses. Making those standards mandatory would establish a nationwide minimum safety floor instead of leaving compliance largely voluntary.
I’d say that’s probably the biggest change here: we aren’t talking about a new e-bike technology or a new battery chemistry. We’re talking about taking safety standards that much of the reputable e-bike industry already follows and making them the baseline for everyone selling these products in America.

title: Review: Volvo's 2028 XC60/90 PHEVs get 80 miles of EV range, changing the game
content:
Volvo flew us out to Copenhagen to drive across the bridge to Sweden to check out the upcoming 2028 XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. The new vehicles promise to double the EV-only range to 73-78 miles, making them a new breed of hybrid rarely seen outside China. But what can you do with so much EV-only range?
At Electrek, we’re usually pretty skeptical of plug-in hybrids. Too many are glorified gas cars with 20-mile batteries that owners often don’t bother to charge. The electric-only powertrain is often underpowered and not something you can actually use day-to-day.
Volvo’s upcoming 2028 XC60 T8 and XC90 T8 “Long-Range” PHEVs are the rare exception that actually force us to pay attention. By stuffing a 41.2 kWh floor-mounted battery (37.9 kWh usable) into its solid but aging SPA1 platform, Volvo has more than doubled the electric range of its two bestselling SUVs. Both now have more battery capacity and range than the original all-electric Nissan Leaf, Hyundai Ioniq, and many of the compliance EVs that followed. Volvo also doubled the charging speed from 3.6kW to a more reasonable 7.2 kW, meaning charge times are roughly unchanged.
The Powertrain: Finally enough battery to matter
Both the XC60 and XC90 share the exact same T8 AWD hardware: a 247-hp 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder up front with a 70-hp front e-boost motor, and an upgraded 174-hp electric motor on the rear axle. Combined output lands at a healthy 455 horsepower and 560 lb-ft of torque.
The real headline, though, is the electric range:
- 2028 XC60 T8: Up to 78 miles of preliminary EPA-estimated EV range (590 miles combined) and 67 MPGe.
- 2028 XC90 T8: Up to 73 miles of preliminary EPA-estimated EV range and 61 MPGe.
Those numbers easily crown both Volvos as the longest-range plug-in hybrids coming to the U.S. market, blowing past the Mercedes-Benz GLE 450e, Toyota RAV4 Prime, and Range Rover PHEVs, which top out around 50 miles. With the average American commuting around 30 to 40 miles a day, you can genuinely treat either of these SUVs like a full EV Monday through Friday without waking up the gas engine once…or so it would appear on paper.
Sadly, there are some caveats to consider that will make these a little harder to run EV-only. First, to accelerate quickly off the line or to operate in AWD mode, the gas engine needs to engage. That makes winter driving and spirited driving a gas-usage endeavor. Also, without DC fast charging, the Level 2 charger tops out at 7.2 kW, meaning longer trips will also require gas usage.
On the plus side, even with the cold weather and snow tires, I saw range over 145 kilometers/90 miles on the XC60 when fully charged.
2028 Volvo XC60 T8: The sharper, fresher pick
If you don’t need a third row, the XC60 is easily the more compelling package.
At 4,855 lbs, it’s quick—ripping from 0–60 mph in 4.5 seconds—and surprisingly efficient for a bulky crossover, sipping 48 kWh per 100 miles in electric mode and returning 29 mpg combined once the battery is depleted. Unlike the XC90, the 2028 XC60 also gets a proper visual refresh, complete with a cleaner front fascia, Matrix LED headlights, horizontal taillights, and an updated interior featuring Google Gemini on its not huge but very usable 11.2-inch touchscreen.
It’s also the easier daily driver in tight spaces, with a 37.4-foot turning circle and slightly more first- and second-row legroom than its bigger sibling. The trade-off is utility: you’re limited to 21.1 cu. ft. of cargo space behind the second row and a 3,500-lb towing capacity.
2028 Volvo XC90 T8: The three-row bridge to full EVs
The XC90 is the family hauler for buyers who want a three-row electric SUV but aren’t quite ready to jump into an EX90 or Rivian R1S.
Because Volvo redesigned the battery into a flat, floor-mounted pack, you don’t lose the XC90’s practicality. You still get 6- or 7-passenger seating, 34.5 cu. ft. of cargo room behind the second row (up to 69.4 cu. ft. max), and a serious 5,000-lb towing rating. Even with the extra bulk, it hits 60 mph in 4.9 seconds.
The downside? Efficiency drops to 53 kWh per 100 miles (27 mpg on gas), the third row’s 31.9 inches of legroom is still best reserved for kids, and outside of the new battery and Google Gemini integration, the cabin and exterior are essentially carryovers, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing since we love Volvo interiors.
The big EV caveats:
Top comment by dashpool
There are plenty of decently-long-range PHEVs available in Europe comparable to these things (e.g. VWAG's ones); it isn't only China. Also, a lot of them are far more affordable (and thus a reasonable alternative for people looking to save on motoring costs).
Availability isn't the issue so much as finding anyone who is interested in both owning and plugging in a PHEV. Almost anyone who is serious about minimising fuel use just gets a BEV instead.
Even with a 41.2 kWh pack, you can’t completely hide the compromises of a plug-in hybrid:
- No fast charging in sight: Refilling that 37.9 kWh usable pack takes 5.7 hours on a standard U.S. Level 2 home charger—and a painful 27 to 53 hours on a regular 120V wall outlet. I don’t hate this because on trips and other times that you need quick range, you’ll just jump into gas mode, but it would be nice to have DC fast charging
- RWD-only in EV mode: Because the gas engine (plus an EV helper motor that can’t operate on its own) powers the front wheels and the main electric motor drives the rear, running in pure EV mode means you’re driving a rear-wheel-drive SUV. In winter weather, demanding all-wheel-drive traction forces the gas engine to kick on. So does gunning it at a green light and the motor stays on for a bit.
- Double the complexity: You’re still maintaining an 18-gallon fuel tank, a turbocharged four-cylinder, and an 8-speed automatic transmission alongside a full EV battery pack. More to haul around, more space taken up and more to go wrong.
- Not a direct EV issue but the Volvo SP1 doesn’t do wireless Carplay/Android Auto natively. You’ll need to plug into USB-C or buy a third party dongle to connect wirelessly. The upside is that Google’s Android in Volvo center stack has most of the same apps as your phone and a fast, native display vs the lag sometimes felt in projection systems.
Electrek’s Take
Look, we’d still rather see buyers go all-electric with the upcoming EX60 or EX90, and if Volvo prices these 2028 T8s too close to $70,000–$80,000 when deliveries start in early 2027, going full BEV will still be a no-brainer in my book.
But for those who aren’t ready to make the leap to full EV, these vehicles are incredibly compelling. Every morning, assuming you’re on a Level 2 charger, you have almost 80 miles of EV range, about double the average American daily usage. Then, of course, the backup of the 18-gallon tank and gas motor for those edge cases like trips or towing in cold weather are covered.
So the takeaway: if you’re going to build a plug-in hybrid in 2027, this is how you do it. Giving drivers 73 to 78 miles of real electric range turns the gas engine from a daily necessity into a road-trip range extender. For households with a Level 2 home charger that still have lingering charging anxiety on long highway trips, the 2028 XC60 and XC90 T8 are easily the smartest PHEVs on the market. Not to mention the smooth, quick and safe rides Volvo is known for.

政策分类依据: 日本第30次FIP光伏拍卖结果，属溢价机制电价支持机制
content:
Markets & Policy
Japan has selected seven PV projects ranging in size from 500 kW to 20 MW in its latest procurement exercise. The lowest bid came in at JPY 5.00 ($0.031)/kWh, while the weighted average final price reached JPY 9.13/kWh.
Emiliano Bellini
27 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
A small ground-mounted PV plant operated by Sun Village in Japan
Japan’s Organization for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO) has announced the results of the country’s 30th auction for utility-scale solar projects.
The procurement exercise allocated 27.7 MW of PV capacity against a target of 91 MW. It was open to solar projects with a generation capacity of at least 250 kW under Japan’s feed-in premium (FIP) scheme.
Eight projects totaling 41.4 MW qualified to participate in the auction. However, only seven projects totaling 27.7 MW submitted bids, with all seven securing support.
The lowest bid of JPY 5.00 ($0.031)/kWh was submitted by Japanese solar installer Marushin Koei for a 500 kW project.
The highest bid of JPY 9.60/kWh, corresponding to the auction’s ceiling price, was submitted by two developers – Machiokoshi Energy and Solar Field 13 – for projects with capacities of approximately 20 MW and 1.3 MW, respectively.
Solar Field 13 also secured support for two 1.99 MW solar projects at JPY 7.50/kWh each. The remaining two projects, with capacities of 888.8 kW and 1 MW, were awarded at JPY 6.99/kWh and JPY 9.50/kWh, respectively.
The weighted average final price came in at JPY 9.13 ($0.057)/kWh.
The auction was the third procurement exercise conducted in Japan’s 2026 fiscal year. It follows the
29th solar auction
, which allocated 38.2 MW at an average price of JPY 8.89/kWh, and the
28th auction
, which awarded 89.2 MW at an average price of JPY 6.74/kWh.
In the 27th auction, the Japanese authorities allocated 79 MW of PV capacity at an average price of JPY 4.61/kWh.
The latest results mark the second consecutive decline in awarded capacity and the second consecutive increase in weighted average prices during the current fiscal year.
Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) confirmed in March that it would
discontinue auction-based support for large-scale solar
after fiscal 2026, while maintaining incentives for smaller PV installations and rooftop solar.
In October, the Japanese authorities
proposed four categories of commercial solar projects
that could continue to benefit from priority government support, including solar installations on publicly owned land and solar carports.
Earlier this month, Japan’s Agency for Natural Resources and Energy (ANRE)
set Dec. 11 as the deadline for new and amended feed-in tariff (FIT) and feed-in premium (FIP) certification applications
for solar installations with capacities of 10 kW and above seeking approval in the current fiscal year, which ends on March 31, 2027. Projects participating in FIP auctions remain subject to separate procurement deadlines.
Japan is also seeking to shift public support toward emerging PV technologies, with the government
prioritizing perovskite solar over conventional silicon technologies in new subsidy programs
. METI has outlined plans to deploy around 20 GW of perovskite solar capacity by 2040.

title: Greenhushing, PV prices, battery prices and the shifting bottleneck - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Greenhushing reflects a shift towards prioritising environmental performance over public sustainability commitments, as declining solar PV and battery costs strengthen the economic case for corporate decarbonisation. The solar industry’s next phase of growth will depend less on equipment affordability and more on grid access, system flexibility, integration and long-term operational value.
International Solar Energy Society (ISES)
27 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Greenhushing refers to the deliberate practice by companies of downplaying, concealing, or remaining silent about their environmental goals, climate commitments, and sustainability initiatives. It contrasts with greenwashing, whereby companies exaggerate or misrepresent their environmental credentials. This trend is becoming increasingly prevalent among U.S. companies as businesses grow more cautious about the political, legal, and financial risks associated with publicly communicating their environmental commitments.
This growing reluctance to disclose sustainability initiatives does not necessarily reflect a reduction in corporate environmental action. Rather, many companies are shifting toward a more restrained communication strategy, prioritising the implementation of sustainability measures over their public promotion. This distinction is particularly relevant in the context of the declining costs of solar photovoltaics and lithium-ion batteries, which have made renewable energy generation and energy storage increasingly economically attractive. As these technologies become more cost-competitive, companies may have stronger financial incentives to adopt them as part of their operations, even as they become less willing to publicise their climate-related investments and commitments.
Recent academic research examining U.S. publicly listed companies
finds that investors may place greater value on demonstrated environmental performance than on extensive sustainability communication.
Evidence indicates that higher levels of corporate greenhushing
– the gap between environmental performance and public communication – are associated with higher subsequent abnormal stock returns, suggesting that investors may place greater value on demonstrable environmental performance than on promotional communication. A
2025 survey by The Conference Board
found that 80% of surveyed sustainability executives were adjusting their ESG strategies in response to the new U.S. administration.
The next leap in solar energy is not in the PV technology
Solar energy has already won the debate over economic viability
. Now, it must demonstrate its ability to create value for the grid, consumers and investors. The solar energy sector worldwide no longer needs to convince any market that it is competitive. PV modules cost only 5% of what they used to cost 15 years ago, and battery prices are only 9% of what they were in 2010. Solar power is already present in utility-scale generation, rooftop installations, businesses, agribusiness and the broader vision of a cleaner economy. The conversation has evolved.
The next phase of growth will not be defined solely by the number of MW of PV installed or the MWh of batteries deployed. It will depend on the ability to deliver energy predictably, in the right location and at the time the power system needs it most. This represents a shift from scale to intelligence: moving away from simply installing PV systems and feeding electricity into the grid toward generating, storing, managing and delivering value. The solar industry has entered a new phase in which the most important question is no longer, “How much does the equipment cost?” Instead, it is, “What problem does this asset solve, and how can it generate value over time?” Answering that question requires a broader perspective involving grid infrastructure, contracts, operations, capital and regulatory confidence.
The bottleneck is shifting and customers buy performance, not equipment
For years, the industry’s priorities were reducing solar PV and storage equipment costs (mostly PV module, inverter and BESS), expanding financing opportunities and accelerating installations. These factors remain important, but they no longer fully explain a project’s competitiveness. In many regions,
the most valuable and contested asset has become grid connection capacity
. The expansion of distributed generation has brought technical challenges into the spotlight, including reverse power flow, substation capacity, power quality, protection systems, metering and grid management. The challenge is no longer simply how much solar electricity can be generated, but whether the power system can efficiently integrate increasingly distributed and variable sources of energy. Consequently, energy storage, demand response, digitalisation and generation located closer to consumption centres are becoming increasingly important. These technologies are no longer optional additions. They are essential tools for making solar energy work more effectively within the broader electricity system.
This changing landscape is redefining the roles of manufacturers, system integrators and project developers. Customers are no longer looking simply for a solar module, inverter or battery. They want comprehensive solutions combining engineering, software, operations, warranties, financing and clear expectations regarding financial returns. In practice, the market is moving toward selling performance rather than individual components. This requires a supply chain better equipped to manage long-term contracts, maintenance, replacement parts, safety, power quality, taxation and logistics. Competitive advantage will increasingly depend on integrating these different elements without transferring unnecessary complexity to customers.
The conversation with consumers is also changing. For industrial companies, solar energy combined with storage can provide greater cost predictability and operational security. For commercial businesses, it can reduce exposure to electricity price peaks and supply interruptions. For agricultural operations, it can reduce vulnerability to logistical and energy-related disruptions. For residential consumers, it is becoming more and more the cheapest and safest option. The real value of technology emerges from how it performs in everyday operations, not simply from the specifications listed in a product catalogue.This transformation also demands more sophisticated supply chain management. Product availability alone is insufficient. Companies need inventory planning, technical assistance, replacement capabilities and the ability to anticipate changes in international trade.
Infrastructure is once again at the centre of the industry’s strategic priorities. Expanding transmission capacity is essential, but it cannot replace distribution planning or independently resolve short-term grid constraints. Location, access to the grid, contractual arrangements and consumption profiles are becoming just as important as the cost of electricity generation. For investors and developers, this means adopting a more comprehensive approach to due diligence. Assessing solar resources, permits and equipment prices is no longer sufficient. Projects must also be evaluated based on grid capacity,
curtailment risks
, contractual structures, capital costs and the value of electricity at different times of the day.
Without integration between planning, market structures and execution, solar expansion risks creating valuable assets in the wrong locations. With proper integration, however, the industry can establish a more resilient growth platform, combining generation, flexibility and demand rather than treating each component as an isolated opportunity. This represents the definitive transition from solar energy as a piece of equipment to solar energy as strategic infrastructure. It is also the pathway toward a more reliable, competitive and resilient industry, prepared to grow sustainably and consistently.
Greenhushing and the declining costs of PV modules and battery storage reflect two sides of the same market transformation: companies can increasingly capture the economic benefits of the energy transition without necessarily promoting their sustainability commitments publicly. This trend is unfolding against a backdrop of growing political uncertainty, further highlighted by the failure of COP31 negotiations in Antalya, where the European Union, the United Kingdom and several other countries rejected the proposed final agreement, arguing that it failed to adequately address the urgency of climate change and did not explicitly mention fossil fuels. The lack of consensus exposes the widening gap between the need for accelerated climate action and the international political capacity to deliver it.
As PV and battery prices continue to fall, the industry’s competitive bottleneck is shifting from equipment affordability to grid access, system flexibility, integration and operational performance. This creates an environment in which corporate adoption may continue to accelerate even as public ESG communication becomes more cautious and international climate negotiations struggle to deliver stronger commitments. Competitive advantage increasingly depends not on how much solar and storage capacity companies install, but on how effectively they deploy, manage and monetise these assets. In this evolving landscape, the value of the energy transition may increasingly be measured by what companies deliver rather than what they declare, particularly as market economics and technological progress continue to advance independently of the pace of political consensus.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: BP, Iberdrola start operations at Spain’s largest green hydrogen plant - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, Australia and Germany are exploring hydrogen-based aviation, while Envision Energy and Greensteel Australia are considering a 400 MW green hydrogen system for low-carbon steelmaking.
Sergio Matalucci
27 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Hydrogen
Utility-scale
25MW green hydrogen plant at bp’s Castellón refinery
Iberdrola
have started operations at their
25 MW green hydrogen plant
at BP’s Castellón refinery, which supplies fuels to customers in Spain and across Europe. The facility, currently Spain’s largest operational green hydrogen plant, is expected to produce around 2,800 metric tons of green hydrogen per year. Iberdrola supplies the plant with 170 GWh of renewable electricity per year from its Spanish wind and solar farms under a power purchase agreement (PPA). The facility features five 5 MW proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzers supplied by Plug Power.
Australia
have expanded their
hydrogen cooperation
to jointly develop value and supply chains for hydrogen-based aviation. Research institutes from the two countries are working with industry partners under the Sustainable Aviation Hub with Australia (SAvHAus) initiative. The project focuses on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production from synthesis gas and ethanol, efficient hydrogen supply, and fuel cell systems. “The project has a funding volume of 9.5 million euros and will run until the end of August 2030,” said the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE), which coordinates the project.
Fraunhofer IWU
has compared the cost-effectiveness of
hollow embossing rolling
with that of conventional hollow embossing, finding that the total cost of a metallic bipolar half-plate falls from €1.13 ($1.24) to €0.82 in its reference scenario. Manufacturing costs excluding materials fall from €0.77 to €0.47 per plate, a reduction of around 39%. In hollow embossing rolling, a thin metal strip undergoes incremental forming between profiled rolls, eliminating the time required to feed the strip and open and close the press. The cost savings also stem from higher throughput. “Accounting for downtime, reduced output, and scrap, hollow embossing achieves an adjusted throughput of 35 bipolar half-plates per minute in the scenario analyzed. Hollow embossing rolling reaches 82 plates per minute,” said the German research institute.
Envision Energy
has announced a strategic partnership with
Greensteel Australia
to explore the deployment of an initial 400 MW green hydrogen system and an integrated renewable energy supply for
low-carbon iron and steelmaking
in New South Wales. Greensteel Australia is developing what it describes as the country’s first new steel mill in more than 30 years. Envision said the next stage would focus on extending the value chain upstream through green hydrogen-based direct reduced iron (DRI) production and electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking. The two stages would explore synergies in green iron and semi-finished steel supply, processing, and logistics, subject to technical and commercial assessments and regulatory approvals.

€17.14 billion electricity transmission network development plan
through 2030, allocating 12.4 GW of additional grid capacity to electricity demand from renewable hydrogen production and its derivatives. The plan aims to accommodate 47.4 GW of new electricity demand across industry, hydrogen production, data centers, housing, and transport. The investment program includes 6,707 km of new transmission lines, upgrades to 8,164 km of existing lines, and 193 new substation sites.

content:
Markets & Policy
Bangladesh’s new Special Solar Power Installation Act requires manufacturers, suppliers and service providers to implement take-back schemes for end-of-life solar equipment, marking a step toward sustainable PV waste management.
Syful Islam
27 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
The government of Bangladesh has made the recycling and disposal of waste generated by solar installations mandatory for manufacturers, suppliers and service providers under its Special Solar Power Installation Act, 2026.
The country’s parliament recently passed the legislation, with a gazette notification issued on Nov. 22.
Under the act, manufacturers, suppliers and service providers of solar panels and related equipment will be responsible for recycling equipment that reaches the end of its operational life or is damaged in accidents or natural disasters.
“A ‘Take-back Scheme’ will be implemented by the concerned manufacturer, supplier, or service provider to take back and manage machinery and equipment of the special solar power system when they become expired or unfit for use,” the act says.
The legislation also stipulates that a tripartite agreement will be signed between the consumer, the service provider and the relevant authority.
Bangladesh currently has no standalone policy governing the management of solar panel and related equipment waste. In its Renewable Energy Policy 2025, the Power Division said provisions for the sustainable disposal and recycling of batteries and PV panels would be incorporated into e-waste regulations by the Ministry of Environment.
Alamgir Hussain, a garment factory owner in Dhaka, welcomed the government’s initiative, warning that improperly managed solar waste could pose significant risks in the coming years.
“Many factories and private building owners are installing solar systems in the rooftops as the government declared incentives for the same. The wastes need proper disposal to avoid hazard,” he said.
Imran Chowdhury, deputy director (PIM) for Bangladesh at ib vogt APAC, said the rapid expansion of the global solar industry is shifting the discussion beyond capacity additions and cost competitiveness toward lifecycle sustainability and responsible solar asset management.
“In this context, it is encouraging to see Bangladesh addressing solar e-waste management through its new Special Solar Power Installation Act, 2026,” he told
pv magazine
Chowdhury said discussions in Bangladesh’s solar industry have largely focused on expanding installed capacity, with relatively little attention paid to managing solar equipment at the end of its operational life.
“The introduction of a Take-back Scheme is particularly noteworthy,” he added.
Given Bangladesh’s heavy reliance on imported solar equipment, however, Chowdhury said the practical implementation of the provision would be critical, particularly regarding whether international manufacturers would establish local take-back arrangements or whether responsibility would ultimately fall on local suppliers, distributors or project investors.
He added that clarity over who would bear the costs of collection, transportation, recycling and disposal would be equally important from an investor’s perspective, particularly for projects developed under the opex model.
“Furthermore, as Bangladesh aims to significantly scale up its renewable energy capacity, I believe a broader solar e-waste management framework covering utility-scale solar projects will also be necessary, particularly considering the volume of solar equipment these projects will bring into the country,” said Chowdhury.

title: Elco launches propane air-to-water heat pumps for commercial applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The new heat pump series is available in seven versions with heating capacities ranging from 40.1 kW to 84.4 kW and seasonal coefficients of performance of up to 4.70. The systems can deliver flow temperatures of up to 75 C and be cascaded to reach a combined capacity of 1.35 MW.
Emiliano Bellini
27 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Heat pumps
The Aerotop Evo P heat pump
Elco, a unit of Italy-based heating system manufacturer
, has introduced a new series of air-to-water heat pumps for space heating, cooling and domestic hot water production in commercial buildings.
“Designed for commercial heating applications, the new air-to-water R290 heat pump combines high efficiency with a modular design, offering outputs from 40 kW to 84 kW and up to 1,344 kW in cascade,” the company said in a statement.
Dubbed Aerotop Evo P, the new product line uses propane (R290) as the refrigerant, with a global warming potential (GWP) of 0.02, and features inverter-driven compressors that adjust their output to match heating and cooling demand.
The heat pumps are available in seven sizes with nominal heating capacities of 40.1 kW, 46.8 kW, 50.4 kW, 55.8 kW, 61.0 kW, 70.2 kW and 84.4 kW.
Their coefficient of performance (COP) ranges from 3.71 to 3.92 at an outdoor temperature of 7 C and a water temperature of 35 C. At the same outdoor temperature and a water temperature of 55 C, the COP ranges from 2.55 to 2.74.
The seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) ranges from 4.22 to 4.70 at 35 C and from 3.41 to 3.63 at 55 C. The systems achieve energy efficiency ratings of A++ or A+++ at 35 C and A++ at 55 C.
In cooling mode, the heat pumps deliver capacities ranging from 34.9 kW to 72.7 kW at an outdoor temperature of 35 C and a water temperature of 7 C. Their seasonal energy efficiency ratio (SEER) ranges from 4.36 to 5.47.
The systems can operate at outdoor temperatures as low as -20 C and achieve a maximum flow temperature of 75 C at an ambient temperature of -5 C under partial-load conditions.
The five smaller models measure 2,384 mm x 2,240 mm x 1,094 mm and have operating weights ranging from 714 kg to 760 kg. The two largest versions measure 3,402 mm x 2,240 mm x 1,094 mm and weigh 1,021 kg each.
The smaller units use a single compressor and contain between 4.5 kg and 4.9 kg of propane, while the two largest models feature two compressors and a total refrigerant charge of 10 kg.
The heat pumps have standard-mode sound power levels ranging from 75 dB(A) to 79 dB(A). Two additional operating modes can reduce sound power levels by up to 10 dB(A), although at the expense of maximum heating and cooling capacity.
The systems also feature refrigerant leak detection sensors, an ATEX-certified extraction fan and a degasser. Operating data can be accessed via a human-machine interface (HMI) or the Modbus communication protocol.
Up to 16 units can be connected in cascade to achieve a combined heating capacity of approximately 1.35 MW. The heat pumps can also be deployed in hybrid configurations alongside existing gas or oil boilers.

content:
Markets & Policy
Wood Mackenzie expects EU funding restrictions on projects using inverters from high-risk suppliers to reduce cumulative solar and energy storage installations across the bloc by 3% between 2027 and 2030. Limited local product availability, rising costs, and supply chain constraints are among the main challenges.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
27 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Inverters
Utility-scale solar and energy storage projects receiving EU funding account for most of the affected capacity.
Wood Mackenzie expects EU restrictions on inverters from high-risk suppliers to reduce cumulative solar and energy storage installations across the European Union by 3% between 2027 and 2030. Utility-scale solar and energy storage projects receiving EU funding account for most of the affected capacity.
In April 2026, the European Commission
introduced restrictions on the use of inverters from high-risk suppliers
in solar and
energy storage projects receiving EU funding
. The measures were implemented through internal guidelines for European financial institutions in response to concerns over cybersecurity and the security of energy infrastructure.
Utility-scale solar and energy storage projects receiving EU funding account for most of the affected capacity. Around 14% of European solar projects and 10% of energy storage projects rely on EU-backed loans or funds.
Wood Mackenzie said exposure is particularly high in Central and Eastern Europe due to the region’s greater reliance on EU funding and the strong presence of Chinese manufacturers. All China-based inverter manufacturers are affected by the country’s designation as a high-risk jurisdiction. Chinese suppliers accounted for more than 80% of European inverter shipments in 2025, with higher market shares in price-sensitive markets that rely more heavily on EU funding.
The research firm assessed the impact of the restrictions through interviews and surveys involving more than 30 industry stakeholders, including manufacturers, suppliers, distributors, solar and storage developers, and national solar associations. The study examines product availability, price increases, and contract renegotiations resulting from supplier changes.
Under its base-case scenario, Wood Mackenzie expects PV installations in key Central and Eastern European markets between 2027 and 2030 to be 6% lower than previously forecast. Energy storage installations are expected to be 5% lower on average. Romania, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria are expected to be the hardest-hit markets due to their high exposure to EU funding restrictions.
The impact is expected to be less pronounced across the European Union as a whole. Wood Mackenzie forecasts a 3% reduction in cumulative solar and storage installations between 2027 and 2030. Western European markets are better positioned to absorb cost increases and have more established commercial relationships with inverter manufacturers not classified as high-risk suppliers. The impact is expected to peak in 2027, when Western supply chains will still have limited capacity to respond to the restrictions.
Wood Mackenzie estimates that inverter manufacturing capacity from suppliers not classified as high risk and available to the European market will exceed 150 GW by the end of 2027. This would be sufficient to meet European demand for solar and storage inverters, although actual availability will depend on distribution networks, logistics, after-sales services, and manufacturers’ ability to fulfill orders in individual markets.
Local product availability is one of the main challenges in Central and Eastern Europe. Some industry stakeholders said Western manufacturers could need months or even years to establish adequate distribution and after-sales service networks. Lead times for large orders could also increase, potentially delaying utility-scale projects.
However, the
European Solar Manufacturing Council (ESMC) recently identified 212 GW of nominal inverter manufacturing capacity
among European and other manufacturers not associated with high-risk countries, compared with EU demand of around 59 GW in 2025. While manufacturing capacity appears sufficient to meet demand, challenges remain in terms of local availability and after-sales services.
Rising costs represent another risk. Some developers said equipment cost increases of 1% to 5% could jeopardize projects with tight margins. Although inverters account for a relatively small share of total project costs, Wood Mackenzie estimates that switching suppliers could increase total system costs for solar and storage projects by 2% to 10%.
The impact is particularly significant for energy storage. A substantial share of battery energy storage systems (BESS) sold in Europe are supplied as AC blocks integrating batteries and inverters from a single manufacturer. Replacing integrated solutions from Chinese suppliers with separate battery and inverter systems could increase costs and complicate installation, system integration, and warranty management. Engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractors and installers surveyed also anticipate additional training costs associated with adopting new inverter models.
Wood Mackenzie also modeled a more severe scenario involving an EU-wide ban on inverters from high-risk suppliers. Under this scenario, cumulative solar and energy storage installations in Central and Eastern Europe between 2027 and 2030 would be more than 18% and 13% below previous forecasts, respectively. Across the European Union, solar installations would be 11% lower and energy storage installations 13% lower, with the largest reductions occurring in 2029 and 2030.
At the time of publication of Wood Mackenzie’s analysis, the European Commission had yet to publish a dedicated document detailing its April 2026 decision.

content:

A Japanese battery storage developer has drawn its first loans for two projects totaling 90 MW after addressing what it says were financing requirements without domestic precedent, tied to price adjustments in the country’s long-term capacity auction contracts.
Brian Publicover
27 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
HEXA Energy Services said this week that MUFG Bank has made initial loan disbursements under project finance agreements for two grid-scale battery energy storage projects in northern and southern Japan, with combined grid connection capacity of 90 MW.
The projects – located in Bibai, Hokkaido, and Kumamoto, Kumamoto prefecture – won capacity contracts in Japan’s
fiscal 2023 long-term decarbonization power auction
. HEXA Energy Services said it “addressed financing requirements without domestic precedent,” including financing terms that reflect contract price adjustments linked to changes in inflation and interest rates.
MUFG Bank said it worked with HEXA Energy Services and other parties “to address the financing considerations specific to the two projects, including those arising from the newly introduced contract price adjustment mechanism under the long-term decarbonization power auction.”
Yoichiro Mizuta, chief executive officer of HEXA Energy Services, said in an online statement that the “financing presented new and significant challenges different from those of our previous projects.” He noted that the initial loan disbursements were completed within about two months.
The company did not disclose the loan amount, tenor, or storage capacity in megawatt-hours of the two projects.
Project pipeline
The financing is HEXA’s third round of project debt for auction-backed batteries. The Tokyo-based company concluded a project finance agreement with MUFG Bank and Société Générale’s Tokyo branch in March 2025 for its 30 MW/130 MWh

in Fukuoka prefecture, with funds disbursed at the end of June 2025. Financing for four projects in Hokkaido and Mie prefecture was disbursed in March 2026, according to the company.
HEXA Energy Services also plans to arrange project finance in its 2026 fiscal year for a battery project in Oyabe, Toyama prefecture. In addition, the company picked up two battery projects in the

in Oita prefecture, supported by a JPY 21.4 billion ($134.2 million) non-recourse refinancing facility arranged by MUFG Bank. Grid access remains the bottleneck: at the end of 2025, about 172 GW of grid-scale battery capacity was at the connection-study stage, against about

title: New record for UK rooftop solar, more growth predicted - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
More than 270,000 solar installations the United Kingdom with six weeks of 2026 still to run. Industry leaders predict further growth in 2027 beyond as new policy support measures strengthen economic case for residential solar.
Matthew Lynas
27 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Certification body MCS has recorded a new annual record for UK rooftop solar installations.
UK solar installers broke the 2025 record for small-scale installations with six weeks of 2026 left to run, backed by growing demand from existing and new build properties.
Certification body MCS recorded 269,195 UK solar installations below 50 kWp capacity in 2025, the strongest calendar year on record. Monthly data shows 260,131 solar installations were recorded in the 10 months to the end of October 2026, with mid-November figures putting deployment ahead of the 2025 annual record.
MCS certification is not a legal requirement for small-scale installations in the United Kingdom, however it is typically required to gain access to utility export tariffs meaning the measure is a strong indicator of residential and small-scale commercial rooftop deployment.
Retrofit installations continue to lead in volume terms, while installations on new build properties accounted for 31% of the total installations in 2026. While this proportion was down on the 37% recorded for 2025, new build properties accounted for approximately 81,000 installations in both years to the end of October.
MCS described the new build market as a key driver of solar growth and noted that new building regulations for homes in England should support even greater deployment. The upcoming Future Homes Standard will mean almost all new homes in England will have solar panels by default from 2028, to comply with more stringent energy efficiency regulations.
MCS also reported record numbers of people investing in more than one technology for their home. The trend is borne out by small-scale battery deployment that is on course to more than double the annual record set in 2025, with an attachment rate of 82%. MCS recorded
73,115 certified battery storage installations
to the end of October 2026, up from 41,460 certified installations in 2025.
Lisa Cooke, managing director of MCS described the 2026 installation figures as “incredible”.
“This shows just how quickly the small-scale renewables industry is growing and leading the UK’s transition to home-grown energy, as more people than ever invest in low-carbon technologies to power their homes,” he said.
Chris Hewett, chief executive of Solar Energy UK also noted that government finance support available through the Warm Homes Loan Scheme should support further deployment growth. The program sees the UK government work with private sector finance partners to de-risk finance for solar and battery storage at the point of sale, giving consumers access to lower interest rates.
“With cheap finance available through the Warm Homes Loan Scheme, alongside rules effectively mandating solar for new homes and buildings entering into force, I have every confidence that even more people will join in the solar revolution next year,” Hewett said.
