title: Warsaw grid operator adds distributed batteries to curb rooftop solar voltage spikes - Energy Storage
content: Warsaw’s distribution system operator (DSO), Stoen Operator, has contracted Polish electrical equipment manufacturer ZPUE S.A. to supply, install, and commission 10 battery energy storage systems across the capital’s distribution network. Each unit is rated at 150 kW and 200 kWh, bringing the combined deployment to 1.5 MW/2 MWh. The systems will be integrated directly alongside 10 medium- and low-voltage transformer substations in neighborhoods with dense concentrations of prosumer rooftop PV. Internal analyses by the DSO in solar-rich zones previously flagged elevated voltage levels and repeated solar inverter disconnections, prompting customer power-quality complaints. By placing storage directly at targeted substations, the operator aims to regulate voltage without disconnecting transformers or upgrading stretches of the urban grid. European cities generally have cables trenches in streets and upgrades are expensive and difficult. “The growing share of renewable energy sources, increasingly dynamic load profiles and the need to modernize infrastructure mean that energy storage is no longer an add-on, but is becoming one of the foundations of modern distribution grids,” said Łukasz Sosnowski, external funding and R&D project manager at Stoen Operator. Site selection weighed local PV density, recorded voltage disturbances, and the physical feasibility of siting units beside existing transformer substations. Beyond voltage control, Stoen expects the fleet to cut network losses, ease local congestion, and open additional hosting capacity for new solar connections. Under the turnkey contract, ZPUE will deliver the battery units, power conversion systems, AC gear, and control and protection equipment, alongside engineering, commissioning, and technical support. The battery cells are rated for up to 7,500 charge and discharge cycles. The project is co-financed by Poland’s National Fund for Environmental Protection and Water Management (NFOŚiGW), which has also been channeling major state grants into utility-scale storage as the country links its balancing market to Europe’s MARI platform . title: Spain’s capacity market alone won’t make batteries bankable, Arup warns - Energy Storage
content: Spain’s capacity market, which launched in June this year, will not be enough on its own to make battery energy storage systems (BESS) bankable, according to a new report from engineering consultancy Arup. While renewables generated 55.5% of Spain’s electricity in 2025, the report says a staggering 5.4 TWh of potential clean generation could not be integrated into the grid. Over the same period, the average impact of grid-balancing and adjustment services on final power prices hit €15.78/MWh, the highest level on record. Arup argues that BESS is the fastest lever to address Spain’s daily flexibility gap, as midday solar output increasingly outstrips demand before load climbs again in the evening. However, the needs of the grid don’t make Spanish BESS bankable for financiers. Drawing on benchmarks from other markets, Arup estimates that Spain’s capacity market could only account for roughly 10% of a battery project’s total income. Developers will therefore need revenue stacking projections across wholesale arbitrage, balancing markets, and congestion management that banks and investors can trust. The estimated 10% is somewhat of a counter to the optimism around the EU-approved capacity mechanism in June, which offered a bankable revenue floor. Under this guidance, lenders remain heavily exposed to merchant and ancillary market volatility. More: Further discussions around this topic was documented in a recent pv magazine panel which was extensively recapped by the Spanish team . “Spain has already proven it can deploy renewables at scale. The next challenge is ensuring all that energy can be used when the system needs it,” said José Cubillo of Arup. “The capacity market is a step forward because it provides greater visibility over part of the revenues, but on its own it does not make a battery a bankable investment.” Cubillo added that developers, investors, and lenders must stress-test project economics across multiple market outcomes rather than relying on a single policy mechanism. Four paths to 2036 Looking out to 2036, Arup maps four scenarios for Spanish storage based on how assets are remunerated and how concentrated ownership becomes. Under “Regulated Champions,” public contracts dominate and large utilities consolidate the market, whereas “Competition by Design” keeps public support while opening the field to independent developers, aggregators, and industrial users. In more market-driven outcomes, “Guardians of the Spread” sees private contracts and vertical integration concentrate batteries among large operators combining generation and retail. Alternatively, “The Algorithmic Bazaar” disperses ownership across smaller actors, shifting competitive advantage toward data, forecasting, and AI-driven trading. Early market activity suggests a hybrid reality is already taking shape: Spain advanced 1.9 GW of storage permits in the third quarter of 2026 and standalone portfolios have begun reaching financial close ahead of the first capacity auctions. title: Aukera Energy reaches financial close on 40.5 MW Scottish solar-plus storage project - Energy Storage
content: Belgium-headquartered renewable energy platform Aukera Energy has reached financial close on its Loch Fergus project in South Ayrshire, Scotland, comprising a 63 MWp solar PV plant co-located with a 40.5 MW battery energy storage system (BESS). The project secured debt financing from French bank Société Générale, covering the construction and operation of the Loch Fergus facility, with commercial operation expected to begin in early 2028. Located around 4km south-east of Ayr, the development combines solar generation and battery storage on a single site, with Aukera Energy confirming both technologies will share grid connection infrastructure. The solar portion secured a 20-year Contract for Difference (CfD) in the UK’s Allocation Round 7a auction earlier this year, which provides long-term revenue certainty for power generation. Meanwhile, the BESS secured a 15-year Capacity Market agreement through the 2029/30 T-4 auction. Aukera Energy has also signed long-term commercial agreements with French utility company EDF. Under a route-to-market agreement, EDF will manage and balance the output from the solar facility, while a separate 12-year optimization contract will enable the battery system to participate in wholesale electricity markets, the Balancing Mechanism and ancillary services. Aukera told ESS News the battery has a two hour duration for a 81 MWh capacity. “Reaching financial close on Loch Fergus marks an important milestone for Aukera, reinforcing our continued investment in the UK market and demonstrating our ability to deliver hybrid energy projects that integrate renewable generation, battery storage and long-term commercial arrangements within a single asset,” said Aiden Yates, managing director at Aukera Energy. “This financing reflects the strength of our approach, and we are grateful to Société Générale for their support throughout this transaction and their confidence in Aukera.” The Loch Fergus project is Aukera Energy’s second co-located solar PV and BESS project in Scotland. Its first hybrid site in the country is the Benthead project, a site that combines 63 MW of solar generation with a 31 MW BESS. “Société Générale is proud to have supported this landmark financing for Aukera’s second co-located solar PV and BESS project in Scotland. Loch Fergus will contribute to a more flexible, resilient and decarbonised UK power system. We look forward to continuing to work with Aukera on future energy transition projects in the UK and Europe,” said Cem Orekli, managing director – energy, mining, industries, Société Générale. Earlier this year, Aukera Energy reached financial close on its 170 MW / 340 MWh Project Volt BESS project in La Louvière, Belgium, with commercial operations expected in mid-2027. title: Germany approves 700 MW/2.8 GWh battery project - Energy Storage
content: The regional authority in Saxony, Germany, said it has approved the construction of a 700 MW/2,800 MWh NESSin Wegefarth, a locality in the municipality of Oberschöna in the district of Mittelsachsen. Danish company CI V Gigastar ProjectCo GmbH has secured planning approval for the project. The battery will be built in two phases on an 11.06-hectare site. The first phase will have 500 MW of power capacity, followed by a second phase adding 200 MW. The two sections will operate as independent units, according to the authority. The project will connect to the transmission grid through a new substation and a 380 kV underground cable linking it to the existing Freiberg Nord substation. Earth berms will mark the facility’s boundaries and provide visual screening, with native shrub hedges planted along their outer sides. To compensate for impacts on nature and the landscape, demolition and land-de-sealing work is planned in the nearby city of Brand-Erbisdorf. The planning approval process considered around 100 objections to the project, including 66 from private individuals and two from nature conservation organizations. The planning decision is due to be published on the authority’s website from Nov. 30 for two weeks. If no legal action is brought during that period, CI V Gigastar ProjectCo can begin implementing the project. The authority said the approval process was a new undertaking for a battery storage project of this scale. The approval marks a step toward increasing power capacity in Saxony, said Béla Bélafi, president of the regional authority. He added that the new storage technology had presented particular challenges for the officials involved in the process. Once completed, the battery is expected to contribute to grid stability. The stored energy could theoretically meet the average daily electricity demand of around 250,000 to 300,000 households, equivalent to the daily demand of a large city such as Chemnitz or Leipzig, said Bélafi. title: 'Germany is now experiencing what other European markets have already been through' - pv magazine Global
content:
Project developers in Germany face at least two difficult years ahead, according to Amós Guillén Duarte, managing director of international project developer FRV in Germany. This is not only due to declining solar revenues and negative electricity prices, but also to a fundamental shift in market conditions.
“The German federal government expects renewable energy deployment to continue with a significantly weaker support scheme,” Duarte told
pv magazine
. In his view, the transition from predictable profitability to lower and less predictable returns is happening too quickly.
Other European markets have already experienced similar changes. In Spain and elsewhere, support schemes have been modified or abolished, resulting in insolvencies and substantial losses. “We are therefore not necessarily wiser, but we have become more cautious,” Duarte said.
Financing is also likely to play an increasingly important role. Portfolio and corporate financing are gaining relevance, particularly for battery storage projects. Bundling projects can facilitate both financing and offtake agreements.
FRV was fully acquired in April 2015 by Abdul Latif Jameel Energy and Environmental Services, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabian family-owned business group Abdul Latif Jameel. FRV is now part of Jameel Energy.
Read the full interview:
Do you see yourselves primarily as a project developer or as an independent power producer (IPP)?
Amós Guillén Duarte, managing director of FRV in Germany:
We see ourselves primarily as an international project developer. After 20 years, however, we have developed the technical and financial capabilities to also become an IPP.
We do not develop projects simply to sell them, although that is part of our business. We select the projects we want to build and operate ourselves. I would therefore describe us as a developer that also sells electricity, rather than a pure IPP.
Our greatest value lies in our own development capabilities and project pipeline. We have managed to evolve from a pure project developer into a company that also operates as an IPP.

However, most IPPs also develop their own projects, and larger developers often retain assets in their portfolios. Where do you draw the line?
It depends on the market. In some countries, such as France, large IPPs often acquire projects at early, mid- or advanced stages of development. In Spain and Australia, our combination of project development and independent power production is relatively unusual. In Germany, it is perhaps more common, as the sector is more fragmented and diversified.
For me, however, the key difference lies in how projects are selected. A developer looking to sell evaluates a project based on its potential sale price. We want to finance and build the project ourselves and generate revenue from electricity sales. That is why we pay particular attention to the markets, technologies and every technical detail.
Until we secure a permit, we try to optimize the design and maximize returns. That does not mean we never sell projects. However, from day one, we assume that we might retain them and try to maximize their value.
How big is FRV?
We have around 3 GW in operation and just over 1 GW under construction, primarily PV and utility-scale battery storage projects. PV accounts for around 85% of the capacity. Our main markets are Spain, Australia, the United Kingdom, Mexico, Germany and Italy. We also have development teams in Chile, Finland and Sweden.
What are your targets in Germany?
Our original target, set in 2025, was around 500 MW of hybrid PV-plus-storage projects and an additional 500 MW of battery storage by 2030. Given the uncertainty surrounding Germany’s Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG), we do not yet know exactly how these projects will need to be designed. It is therefore unclear whether we can achieve all our original targets within that time frame. However, we are working hard to do so.
Do you also acquire projects?
Our focus is on developing our own PV and battery storage projects.
We have recently seen Enerparc’s insolvency and the difficulties facing ABO Energy. How do you view the current situation in Germany?
The situation is not good at the moment. I try to understand the new federal government’s perspective. It seems to assume that renewables have reached maturity and no longer need support. That is a difficult transition in a country where the EEG has provided a very stable market environment until now. It was like a safety net.
Germany has changed direction and is following developments in southern European markets. The federal government expects renewable energy deployment to continue under a much weaker support scheme. I think the transition from guaranteed profitability to lower and less predictable returns is happening too quickly in Germany.
Project developers are the first to be affected. There is no longer a healthy market for early- or mid-stage projects in Germany. The market will remain challenging for at least the next two years.
IPPs are less affected because they have operational assets generating recurring revenue, and electricity prices are currently high.
I would have expected you to mention the cannibalisation of solar power prices and negative prices first.
It’s both. Many changes are happening at the same time and within a very short period. That is exactly what destabilises the market. On top of that, there is another problem: grid operators are restricting grid access.
In the past, even a project that was not yet ready-to-build had value. Now there is no market for such projects anymore, and lenders put the value of a pipeline at zero or a minimal amount.
Yet a company’s value is the value of its existing assets plus the value of its pipeline. That is a heavy blow for developers whose main assets are their pipelines.
If the pipeline hardly counts in valuations any more, does it also become harder to obtain bridge financing or other financing?
Yes, definitely.
How can developers and IPPs respond? What did companies do in Southern Europe, where this development started earlier?
First, diversification helps. If you only develop solar projects, whose value is falling sharply right now, you have a problem. A mix of PV, wind, batteries, hybrid projects and possibly also power supply for data centres is almost essential today.
Second, good cost discipline will be crucial over the next two years. A large developer with many employees and high fixed costs that doesn’t sell any projects during the transition will run into financial trouble very quickly. Smaller companies with a lean cost structure are better placed to get through the coming period.
Third, access to capital matters. Having a bank, a fund or a financially strong owner behind you for support helps enormously compared with being on your own.
I also expect the market to consolidate as smaller companies merge. Germany is characterised by many smaller, regionally active companies. I believe that in a few years there will be fewer but larger players, as in other European markets such as France, Spain or Poland.
You say project pipelines have lost considerable value, yet you continue to invest in development yourselves. Why has their value fallen so sharply, and why are you confident that you can still develop economically viable projects?
In Germany, a pipeline has hardly any tradable value during this transition window. Once we have a new EEG, a new price will emerge. But until then, nobody knows the price and you can’t calculate a return. The key figures may become clear in March or April, after the first auction for PV capacity under the new EEG.
Projects certainly still have value; it just can’t be calculated at the moment. As long as the new rules are unclear and that value can’t be quantified, IPPs, banks and investors have lost some of their appetite. I see this as a temporary problem. The market could pick up again in about one to one and a half years.
In addition, the market for early-stage development has largely disappeared. In the past, a developer could sell a project at various stages: after securing the land, at an advanced permitting stage or as a ready-to-build project. Today, buyers are mainly interested in the third stage, because it lowers their risk when buying.
A fully developed project can still be valuable, but a developer needs money every month to cover the fixed costs of project development until a project reaches a later stage of maturity than it used to.
In the PPA segment, revenues depend on the power market rather than on EEG auctions. Does the problem still affect the PPA segment?
PPAs are not affected to the same extent. In Germany, you can still sign good PPAs at prices above the levelized cost of electricity. But offtakers also take their cue from EEG prices.
If a CfD offers a price of 59 euros per megawatt hour, for example, why would an offtaker pay 79 euros for a PPA? That is why many companies are waiting to see at what prices the next EEG auction clears. A premium for the PPA can then be calculated on that basis. PPAs remain attractive, but there is a waiting period there too at the moment.
The way financing is structured may also change. Will there be more portfolio financing instead of project financing?
Yes, especially for battery storage. Put simply, there are three levels: corporate financing, where a company receives capital and can deploy it itself within certain limits; financing of individual projects; and, in between, portfolio financing. This kind of financing via a platform with several projects is growing for battery storage in both Germany and the UK and is gaining ground over single-project financing.
There are two main reasons for this. First, batteries are not easy to finance because the financial model is complex. For small batteries, it isn’t worth it. Today, the financing volume often needs to be at least around 20 to 30 million euros. If a single project only needs ten million euros, it is too small for many lenders. But if you bundle three or four storage systems of, say, 30, 40 or 50 megawatts each, you reach an interesting size.
Second, you can also bundle the offtake. For a tolling agreement with an offtaker, it is often more attractive to offer several storage assets as a portfolio. This lets you secure revenues for several projects and then negotiate financing for the whole package. This works particularly well for smaller battery storage systems.
There are also PV-plus-storage and wind-plus-storage portfolios. Here too, larger volumes generally make financing easier. A portfolio can also combine economically stronger and weaker projects. A single project with a weak IRR or a low debt service coverage ratio might not be financeable. Combined with a very good project, however, the portfolio average may be enough to secure a loan. In this way, it may be possible to finance a larger total capacity. And of course there are synergies and cost advantages from larger volumes with suppliers and in EPC.
Back to your projects in Germany. Do they generally include batteries? If so, you often only get a grid connection for storage that may only be charged with green electricity. Is that acceptable for you?
In our view, a PV-only plant without storage is almost a dinosaur these days. Since around the middle of last year, our rule has been to develop new PV projects only with batteries, unless we see an exceptionally attractive PPA.
What we want is a PV plant with a battery storage that is also allowed to draw power from the grid. In Spain, you often get good import capacity. In Germany, this is unusual. Hardly any import capacity is granted for hybrid projects. That reduces profitability.
Grid operators are often reluctant to commit to both feed-in capacity for the PV plant and import capacity for the battery right from the start. If the developer later proves that it is actually investing in the PV plant, the grid operator may be willing to provide an additional 20, 30 or 40 percent of the feed-in capacity as import capacity. That is a risk worth taking, because the business case works without the import capacity too, just not as well.
Having both commitments before the project starts would be ideal. But anyone in Germany who waits and only develops projects that have both a positive, firm grid connection commitment for feed-in and an import commitment from day one will hardly make any progress. These grid connections are scarce.
Timing also helps us with the numbers: we develop for commissioning in about two to three years. By then, batteries should be cheaper, and more storage in the power system could ease negative prices. You can’t assess a project that won’t be connected to the grid for another two years solely on the basis of today’s market conditions.
Are you able to do this precisely because you have more equity available and don’t necessarily have to rely on as much debt in a project? And developers who aren’t in that position can’t develop such projects?
One of my concerns is that you can’t build seven, eight or ten gigawatts of PV without lenders. Equity alone won’t do it. And if people think a very low CfD price of 5.9 cents per kilowatt hour, or now perhaps 6.3 cents, is good for the country, I would argue that the next EEG auction could end up undersubscribed. The build-out of EEG plants could decline or come to a complete halt in 2027.
I don’t think the level mentioned, around 6.3 cents per kilowatt hour, is attractive enough for Germany once you adjust for hours with negative prices and possible future grid fees.
My fear is that the German government will start with a ceiling price that is too low. If an auction is undersubscribed, it will have to raise the price next time and then raise it again. In the past, support started high and was gradually reduced. Now the direction could reverse. We might lose time as a result but perhaps end up with a more appropriate price. Those are the two sides of the coin.
Back to cannibalisation and negative power prices. Both also exist in Spain and other countries.
Negative prices and a temporary oversupply of renewable energy are not a German phenomenon. We see this in Spain, France, Italy, Romania and other countries.
The most important difference is the experience companies have. Germany had a very stable market for a long time. The EEG provided a reliable floor. In Spain and other countries, on the other hand, we have seen cuts to support, abrupt rule changes, insolvencies and heavy losses. This led to legal disputes worth billions. In countries such as Romania, Poland and Hungary, support schemes like green certificates were also changed or abolished. Many companies ran into difficulties as a result. So we are not necessarily smarter, but we have become more cautious.
In Spain, there have been no successful auctions for years. Over six years, 40 gigawatts were added, largely through private PPAs with the associated market and price risks. Germany is now trying to move in this direction.
The problem is that, at the same time, the EEG is being reformed, prices are under pressure, there are more hours with negative prices, and new grid fees are being discussed, including for PV. If, for example, I don’t know whether the grid fees for a project will be 4,000 or 7,000 euros per megawatt per year, the difference is far too large for bankable financing.
This is not one or two changes in a row, but six or seven within roughly a year and a half. It is completely understandable that German project developers and IPPs are worried and holding back.
Once the EEG, the grid package and the AgNes grid fee reform are settled, it will be possible to run the numbers again. Other countries have, to some extent, got used to political and regulatory uncertainty. Germany comes from a different environment.
How do you deal with the uncertainty in Spain?
With patience, and by adding batteries to existing plants. In Spain, there are grid nodes, especially those with connected solar and wind systems, where around half of the possible electricity generation is at times curtailed in spring and autumn. At some sites, it is even more. That’s unfair, but we are adapting to this aggressive environment one way or another.
But surely you can’t build batteries for all of the curtailed power?
Not for all of it. But Spain is now responding to these bottlenecks. In March, we applied to retrofit batteries with grid charging at several existing PV plants. Within a few months, we received commitments for import capacity covering a large share of the plants’ capacity. Grid operators can see that otherwise huge amounts of electricity are lost every year. Additional storage can rescue the economics of existing plants. This new storage capacity certainly comes at a price, but it reshapes the projects’ economics and restores them.
Without a solution, some operators could go bankrupt within three years. That is why there is great time pressure in Spain. In Germany, by contrast, there has long been the certainty of being compensated for curtailment or redispatch.
Germany is facing a paradigm shift and moving closer to market conditions like those in France, Italy or Spain. But there is still a long way to go from where things stand today. We bring experience from countries that have already been through such upheavals and try to apply it to Germany. Next year will still be difficult. This transition phase is interesting, but sometimes frustrating too. Once the rules are set and the storm has passed, there will be a new starting point. I am convinced that renewable energy has a great future in Germany.

title: Tongwei signs 846 MW module deal for Romania's Dama Solar project - pv magazine Global
content:
Tongwei and Rezolv Energy recently signed an agreement to supply 846 MW of Tongwei TNC 3.0 modules for Dama Solar in Romania, set to become one of Europe’s largest single-site solar plants.
The project will have an installed capacity of 1.36 GWp and is expected to generate around 1,800 GWh of electricity a year once operational, making it a major addition to Romania’s renewable power supply.
The agreement was signed during a visit to Tongwei by senior representatives from Actis and Rezolv Energy, including Rezolv Energy CEO Alastair Hammond. Liu Shuqi, Chairwoman and CEO of Tongwei Co., Ltd., welcomed the delegation. Discussions covered the project’s strategic planning and developments in Europe’s renewable energy market.
What it takes to power a gigawatt-scale project
Tongwei is a global leader in high-purity polysilicon and solar cells, with an integrated photovoltaic business spanning silicon production, cell and module manufacturing, and solar power plant development. The project partner, Rezolv Energy, is an independent renewable energy producer established by Actis in 2022, focusing on project development and long-term operation across Central and Southeastern Europe.
Located in Arad County in western Romania, Dama Solar’s scale and long operating life place higher demands on module efficiency, environmental adaptability, and long-term reliability.
To meet these requirements, the project will use Tongwei’s TNC 3.0 modules. Combining advanced solar cell technology with a quarter-cut cell design, the modules deliver high power output while supporting operational reliability and stable electricity generation over the long term.
Alongside module technology, Tongwei’s vertically integrated manufacturing system supports quality management throughout production. The company is organizing production and coordinating supply in line with Dama Solar’s requirements. “We will draw on our integrated manufacturing system to strengthen coordination with our partners across technology, supply and project execution, supporting Europe’s energy transition with high-efficiency, reliable products, and professional services,” said Liu Shuqi, Chairwoman and CEO of Tongwei Co., Ltd.
The first truckload of modules for Dama Solar has departed Tongwei’s Nantong manufacturing facility, marking the start of deliveries under the agreement.
Dama Solar adds to Tongwei’s utility-scale solar business in Europe and its work with international infrastructure investors and renewable energy developers. The project combines the partners’ expertise in renewable energy development, manufacturing, and supply.

title: Hong Kong researchers build 27.04%-efficient perovskite solar cell via trans-interface engineering - pv magazine Global
content:
Scientists at the
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
(HKUST) have developed a perovskite solar cell with a novel interface engineering technique aimed at simultaneously improving power conversion efficiency, operational stability and device-to-device reproducibility.
Dubbed trans-interface engineering (TIE), the proposed approach addresses mechanical failure at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the charge transport layer, which remains a major obstacle to the industrialization of perovskite PV technology.
Conventional interface engineering strategies rely on planar interlayers to passivate defects and improve mechanical interlocking between adjacent layers. These approaches, however, often involve a trade-off between efficient charge transport and interfacial stability.
To overcome this limitation, the researchers developed vertically aligned, mechanically robust nanolinks that penetrate both the perovskite absorber and the charge transport layer, rather than forming a discrete interlayer between them.
As a proof of concept, the research team incorporated trifunctional and monofunctional organic linkers into the perovskite and charge transport layers, respectively. It then used cyanoisopropyl radicals derived from azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN) to initiate polymerization of the organic linkers within their respective layers.
This radical-mediated process also enables the linkers to form vertical bonds across the heterointerface, creating a covalently interconnected structure that reportedly facilitates charge transfer while improving resistance to mechanically induced degradation.
The resulting interface exhibited superior mechanical reliability compared with previously reported interface engineering approaches. The researchers attributed this improvement largely to the suppression of interfacial mechanical failure during device operation.
The best-performing solar cell fabricated with the proposed technique achieved a power conversion efficiency of 27.04%, with a certified value of 26.67%. The name of the certification body was not disclosed.
Under maximum power point (MPP) tracking and one-sun illumination, 92% of the tested devices achieved T80 lifetimes of at least 1,400 h. The T80 metric indicates the time required for a solar cell’s efficiency to decline to 80% of its initial value.
The scientists emphasized that the high proportion of devices reaching the reported T80 lifetime demonstrates not only improved operational stability but also higher reproducibility across individual devices, a key requirement for industrial-scale manufacturing.
They also noted that the proposed trans-interface engineering approach could be extended to other multilayer optoelectronic devices beyond photovoltaics.
The new cell design was presented in the study “
Trans-interface engineering for reliable perovskite solar cells with reproducible stability
,” published in
nature photonics

title: Kenya records $576 million in Chinese solar cell imports from January-October - pv magazine Global
content:
Kenya is becoming a leading destination for Chinese solar cells, as well as an export hub for solar parts bound for markets including the US and Indonesia, trade data indicate.
China exported $576.1 million worth of solar cells to Kenya between January and October 2026, according to figures first cited by Bloomberg.
The figure traces back to China-Kenya Trade 2026 statistics available through online platform ChinaData, sourced from the China General Administration of Customs. The platform records an 11,214.5% increase in the value of solar cells exports from China to Kenya over the first ten months of this year when compared to the same period in 2025.
Chinese solar cell exports to Kenya totalled $7.7 million across the whole of 2025, ChinaData’s figures show, compared to $4.2 million in 2024, $5.6 million in 2023 and $7.5 million in 2022.
The $576.1 million total represents 10.97% share of China’s solar cell exports over the first ten months of 2026, according to ChinaData. Bloomberg also reported that Kenya was the single biggest importer of Chinese solar parts in October.
Kenya applies a 0% customs import duty to photovoltaic cells, including unassembled cells, according to the East African Community Common External Tariff, a unified import duty schedule that came into effect in July 2022.
Kenya’s national statistics agency, the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), has also noted rising exports of photovoltaic products to markets including the US, Egypt and Indonesia.
In a report published in September covering the second quarter of 2026, KNBS said Kenyan exports to the US had increased substantially, with the growth largely driven by domestic exports of assembled and unassembled solar cells, alongside coffee and maize oil.
The report also noted an increase in domestic exports of unassembled solar cells to Egypt and Indonesia.
Additional data from BloombergNEF indicate that Kenyan solar panel shipments to the US reached $138 million by August 2026, having risen from almost zero in January.
Kenya’s growing role in the solar supply chain comes as solar deployment accelerates across Africa. A
report published by energy think tank Ember
in September forecast that Africa would install a record 17 GW of solar capacity in 2026, equivalent to around 100,000 solar panels per day.
The report also projected that Africa’s solar module manufacturing capacity would quadruple this year. Egypt and Tanzania lead the continent in operational manufacturing capacity, while a further six African countries – Morocco, South Africa, Algeria, Tunisia, Nigeria and Kenya – are expected to add a further 1 GW combined.
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFISA) has tracked 2,593 MW of operational solar in Kenya, according to figures available in its project database, 1,971 MW of which is listed as C&I projects.

title: China polysilicon spot trading thins amid steep futures discounts - pv magazine Global
content:
The China Mono Premium, the OPIS assessment for mono-grade polysilicon used in n-type ingot production, was unchanged week on week at CNY 40.100 ($5.98)/kg, or CNY 0.084/W, according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Nov. 24.
According to market participants, there has been little change in supplier offers and trading conditions in the Chinese polysilicon market, with an increasingly limited number of spot transactions being concluded. A trader said that buyers, having taken delivery of lower-priced orders agreed earlier, were reluctant to resume purchases at manufacturers’ higher asking prices.
Meanwhile, the price spread between the spot and futures markets has remained wide and, in some cases, continued to widen, prompting buyers to shift their procurement towards the futures market.
According to Guangzhou Futures Exchange data for Nov. 23, settlement prices for polysilicon contracts maturing between December 2026 and November 2027 ranged from CNY 30.150/kg to CNY 33.340/kg, with even the highest settlement price across the 12 delivery months standing 16.86% below OPIS’ assessed spot price this week.
Explaining the widening spread, one industry participant said that while manufacturers involved in the industry’s self-discipline agreement on pricing and sales appeared to remain committed to its terms, growing difficulties in selling their output had left them with little choice but to offer more polysilicon into the futures market.
Against this backdrop, market rumors have recently circulated that a trading company may be planning to purchase polysilicon inventories held by manufacturers in a coordinated buying arrangement. Although no official confirmation has emerged, accounts suggest that the trading company would acquire manufacturers’ inventories at prices in the CNY 30s/kg range and subsequently resell the material once prices recover to the CNY 40s/kg range.
An industry participant cautioned that, as with previous attempts to support the industry during periods of prolonged weakness, the success of such an initiative would depend on how acquisition costs and profits from subsequent sales were allocated among the parties involved. Polysilicon manufacturers would have little incentive to support the arrangement if the trading company were to retain all the profits, the source added.
Several industry participants said that a meaningful recovery in the polysilicon market is unlikely in the near term, particularly given the lack of substantial improvement in the supply-demand balance and end-user demand.
One market participant identified persistently high inventory levels and the lack of significant capacity exits as major obstacles to market recovery, noting that there was little indication of any major supplier exiting the market in the short to medium term. Some manufacturers continue to maintain relatively stable cash flows, while others draw financial support from their diversified business operations, with larger producers potentially benefiting from government support, the source added.
The Global Polysilicon Marker (GPM), the OPIS benchmark for polysilicon produced outside China, was assessed at $19.234/kg, or $0.040/W, unchanged from the previous week.
As the year draws to a close, one industry source identified the development of U.S. domestic manufacturing capacity as a key factor that could shape the global polysilicon market in the coming year. The source noted that substantial U.S. solar cell manufacturing capacity is expected to come online progressively in the second quarter of 2027.
Polysilicon suppliers whose materials are used in the wafers procured by these manufacturers are likely to benefit from the resulting demand. In particular, the source expects U.S.-produced polysilicon and wafers, as well as fully Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC)-compliant wafer manufacturing facilities in Vietnam, to see relatively strong demand.
Another industry source cautioned that global polysilicon producers without downstream wafer manufacturing capacity could face greater difficulties in selling their material in 2027. The source pointed out that total polysilicon demand from the U.S. solar market is smaller than the current supply capacity of global polysilicon manufacturers, and that as few as two suppliers could potentially meet the market’s entire requirements. Consequently, producers may increasingly target alternative markets, such as India, although continued price competition with Chinese suppliers is expected to remain a challenge.
OPIS is a specialist business within Dow Jones Energy, a global energy intelligence business that brings together trusted price reporting, research and market intelligence across the energy value chain. OPIS publishes the
OPIS Global Solar Markets Service
, which includes pricing data for solar panels and components across Asia, Europe and the U.S., manufacturing capacity data, module forward curves, and a global solar policy tracker.

title: Rooftop PV could offset 37.3% of vertical farm electricity use - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers from China’s Zhejiang Normal University have investigated the potential of integrating rooftop photovoltaics with vertical farming to improve land productivity, reduce reliance on grid electricity, and ensure economic viability. Their study combines a year-long experiment using flowering plants with simulations across 40 Chinese counties to assess the trade-offs between land use, energy performance, and profitability.
“Vertical farming saves land but multiplies the energy needed for lighting and climate control,” the team explained. “Photovoltaics can supply that energy, but only by taking up land that vertical farming was meant to free. Whether the trade is worthwhile then comes down to what the crop is worth and whether a market exists for it.”
The scientists conducted a 12-month rooftop vertical farming trial in Jinhua, eastern China, from August 2023 to July 2024. They grew 10,500
Hippeastrum
Lemon Sherbet plants in two insulated units, each occupying 17.4 m² and equipped with four 670 W monocrystalline solar modules, for a total installed PV capacity of 2.68 kW per unit.
One unit featured a three-layer configuration with 4,500 plants, while the other featured a four-layer configuration with 6,000 plants. In both units, LEDs provided a 12-hour photoperiod at three daily light integral (DLI) levels of 1.73 mol/m²/day, 2.89 mol/m²/day, and 3.54 mol/m²/day. The temperature was set at 22 C, with a target relative humidity of 60% to 70%. Light intensity was fixed for each shelf.
At harvest, the team measured each bulb at its widest point and compared the results with a greenhouse cultivation benchmark derived from the scientific literature. The researchers also monitored electricity consumption for lighting, climate control, and auxiliary equipment and used the Photovoltaic Geographical Information System (PVGIS) to estimate annual rooftop solar power generation.
They combined the experimental data with modeled energy demand for six combinations of lighting intensity and planting configuration to assess land productivity, annual PV coverage, and financial performance over a 20-year period. They then extended the model to 40 Chinese counties, keeping crop yields constant to assess how local climatic conditions and solar resources would affect energy performance.
“Under real operating conditions, the PV-integrated vertical farm remained energy-intensive while delivering high land productivity and, in five of the six simulated scenarios, a positive net present value,” the researchers said. “Measured consumption reached 691.3 kWh m⁻² yr⁻¹, of which LED lighting accounted for 73.6%, and the estimated hybrid measured-simulated annual energy contribution index (ECI) was 37.3%. Crop selling price and yield drove economic viability far more than electricity price or capital cost in the sensitivity analysis.”
Across all three DLI levels, the four-layer configurations achieved higher land equivalent ratios (LERs) and net present values (NPVs) than their three-layer counterparts. However, they also exhibited higher simulated energy consumption and lower PV coverage. The researchers noted that the lack of randomization in the allocation of lighting treatments across shelves made it difficult to isolate the effects of light intensity from those of shelf position.
Of the six simulated scenarios, a DLI of 2.89 mol/m²/day offered the best trade-off between profitability and annual PV coverage in the case study, with an LER of 29.17, an estimated ECI of 25.4%, and an NPV of CNY 166,886 ($25,040), based on a real discount rate of 2%.
“The land-energy-economy framework revealed the trade-off among the three objectives. In the six simulated scenarios, no configuration maximized land productivity, PV energy coverage, and economic return at once, as ECI fell from 41.5% to 21.9% while LER rose from 20.33 to 29.90,” the group concluded. “Performance across the 40 counties varied mainly with solar resource endowment, at least within this simplified model.”
Their findings are available in the study “
Synergizing land-energy-economy performance in photovoltaic-integrated vertical farming: An empirical study based on year-round
Hippeastrum
cultivation and regional simulations
,” published in
Energy for Sustainable Development
In 2023, scientists at Italy’s Polytechnic University of Marche proposed
combining vertical farming with solar power generation in greenhouses
to improve land utilization and increase agricultural yields. They identified photovoltaics as a promising means of offsetting the high electricity consumption associated with LED lighting in vertical farming facilities. pv magazine Global
More recently, researchers at Mexico’s Northwestern Center for Biological Research (Cibnor) developed a
solar-powered aeroponic system for off-grid vertical farming
. The $719 prototype, equipped with a 50 W solar module, supported two basil harvests during a 55-day cultivation trial.

title: How Push Power used a drone to install rooftop solar at Bentley Motors HQ - pv magazine Global
content:
UK developer Push Power has installed a 2.8 MW rooftop solar installation at Bentley Motors headquarters in Crewe, England, in a project covering four roofs at the manufacturers new paint shop facility.
The installation saw Push Power work with a local partner to deploy a single drone to lift 2,030 solar panels at a height of more than 20 meters. The developer estimates using drones halved the installation time while delivering a safer working environment for engineers, reduced manual handling and, by bypassing diesel-fueled telehandlers, reduced construction vehicle emissions at the site. Push Power reported that lifting panels via drone technology resulted in an installation rate of about one panel per minute, and the full installation was complete in two weeks.
Loading limits on the rooftop presented the main challenge for the installation, according to Push Power. “We couldn’t simply set full pallets down where the installers needed them,” Matt Moss, project manager at Push Power told
pv magazine.
“We delivered panels in small batches as the roof team needed them. That avoided having to unload and redistribute a full pallet on the roof.
Also, of course, the weather in November and the shortness of daylight,” Moss added. “If we had the luxury of doing the work in the summer months, we could have completed in even less time.”
The developer used 515 W JA Solar panels at the site, with each module weighing approximately 30 kg. No modifications to the panels were required, according to Push Power, and each was lifted using a specially designed bag carried by an XAG P150 cargo drone. Push Power told
pv magazine
that crash mats were also used on site as added protection on landing.
Push Power worked in collaboration with AutoSpray Systems and the AutoSpray Pilot Network to complete the drone installation work. AutoSpray operated under its UK Civil Aviation Authority Operational Authorization, issued under UK SORA at SAIL II, with medium containment. A company spokesperson told
pv magazine
this is a “complex area where all procedures were assessed by the Civil Aviation Authority.”
All staff on site were also trained under AutoSpray’s LANTRA competence framework, taking a course called Aerial Logistics. The course trains drone pilots, covering lifting regulations and operational limits, but also the ground teams to prepare loads correctly, attach them correctly, and adhere to regulations.
In a press release, Push Power managing director Andy Khan said the business is always looking for innovative solutions” to optimize and streamline technical operations.
“Devising this new technique of using cargo drones as a faster, saver, cleaner and more efficient way to position rooftop PV panels, we were eager to implement this at the Bentley Motors site and we’re satisfied with the results.”
Andreas Lehe, member of the board for manufacturing at Bentley Motors, added that innovations such as cargo drones “demonstrate how we are finding safer, smarter and more efficient ways to expand our renewable energy infrastructure.”
Ed Clay of remotely piloted aircraft systems at the UK Civil Aviation Authority said the regulator is helping to create the conditions for new technologies to develop safely. “By working with industry to assess and manage risk, we are enabling increasingly advanced drone operations that can deliver practical benefits for businesses and communities across the UK.” Clay said.

title: Estonia switches on 244 MW of solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Estonian renewable energy company Sunly has opened the 244 MW Risti solar park.
The project is Estonia’s largest operational PV plant to date. It spans over 270 hectares, consists of over 340,000 solar panels and is expected to produce enough electricity to meet the annual consumption of nearly 90,000 Estonian households.
The €125 million ($137.1 million) investment was co-financed by the European Investment Bank, SEB and Luminor. As part of a local benefit arrangement, Sunly is paying the local Lääne-Nigula municipality 0.6% of the solar park’s annual electricity sales revenue.
Janno Randmaa, Mayor of Lääne-Nigula Municipality, said the revenue the municipality receives from the solar park’s electricity sales will provide additional resources to support local development. “For us, it is important that projects of this scale also create lasting value for local communities,” Randmaa said.
The solar park marks the first stage of Sunly’s wider development plans for the Risti area. The developer is planning a 42 MW wind farm in the same park, while construction is already underway on a 143 MW/294 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS), developed in cooperation with Rolls-Royce. The battery is expected to start operating next year.
The Risti BESS is one of several Sunly and Rolls-Royce are working on together across the Baltics, with a further four battery storage projects, all in Latvia, also under construction. These projects have a combined capacity of 225 MW/490 MWh and are expected to become operational in 2027.
The two companies have also signed two additional memoranda of understanding outlining intention to enter into long-term service agreements for battery storage projects in Estonia and Latvia.
“Together, we are building the infrastructure needed for a more flexible and resilient energy system,” said Andreas Görtz, President of the Mobile & Sustainable Business Unit at Rolls-Royce.
Estonia’s solar capacity reached around 1.43 GW by the end of 2025 after
adding 105 MW
last calendar year.

title: Reactive UV additive improves back-contact solar module durability - pv magazine Global
content:
A Chinese research team has developed a novel ultraviolet (UV)-converting polyolefin elastomer (POE) encapsulant for back-contact silicon solar modules, with the aim of improving their long-term reliability and mitigating UV-induced and potential-induced degradation (PID).
The researchers sought to overcome the limitations of conventional UV-converting encapsulants, in which physically blended additives can migrate through the polymer matrix, compromising electrical insulation and moisture-barrier properties. To address this issue, they designed a reactive additive capable of forming covalent bonds with the polymer network during module lamination.
“In this study, a reactive down-conversion POE encapsulation film was developed by incorporating the benzotriazole derivative BTBA, which contains polymerizable C=C groups,” the researchers explained. “The disappearance of the C=C absorption band after lamination, together with the subsequent migration and crosslinking results, supports the proposed chemical incorporation and covalent immobilization of BTBA within the POE network.”
The scientists synthesized two benzotriazole derivatives using previously reported procedures: 2-tert-butyl-4,7-bis[4-[(acryloyloxymethyl)methyl]phenyl]-2H-benzotriazole (BTBA), which served as the reactive additive, and 2-tert-butyl-4,7-bis[4-[(1-methylpropoxy)methyl]phenyl]-2H-benzotriazole (BTBM), which served as a physically blended reference additive.
They incorporated BTBA into the POE matrix at concentrations of 0.3 wt%, 0.6 wt%, and 0.9 wt%. They also fabricated reference films containing 0.6 wt% BTBM and baseline films containing neither UV-converting additive.
The team extruded the formulations into 0.45 mm-thick films and used them to encapsulate n-type monocrystalline back-contact solar cells in glass-glass mini-modules. The lamination process involved six minutes under vacuum followed by 10 minutes at 148 C.
The academics used infrared spectroscopy to investigate the curing behavior of BTBA, monitored additive migration at 150 C, and assessed the films’ physical properties and adhesion performance.
They also compared the performance of modules incorporating 0.6 wt% BTBA, 0.6 wt% BTBM, and unmodified POE after 192 hours of PID testing and separate UV-aging tests with a cumulative irradiation dose of 120 kWh/m². Both tests were conducted at a temperature of 85 C and a relative humidity of 85%.
“Compared with the concentration-matched physically blended BTBM formulation, the BTBA-modified POE exhibited markedly suppressed additive migration, a modestly higher bulk crosslinking degree, higher volume resistivity, and better retention of moisture-barrier properties,” the scientists stated. “These results indicate that the chemical incorporation of BTBA helps maintain the structural and functional integrity of the POE encapsulant.”
The modules encapsulated with the BTBA-modified POE exhibited a power loss of 4.11% after 192 hours of PID testing and 1.60% after exposure to a cumulative UV irradiation dose of 120 kWh/m². Both values were lower than those recorded for their BTBM-based counterparts under the same testing conditions.
“Overall, the results support BTBA as a chemically reactive and migration-resistant functional additive for POE encapsulation and indicate that its incorporation can mitigate UV- and PID-related degradation under the accelerated conditions investigated here,” the group concluded.
The novel encapsulant was presented in the study “
Covalently anchored down-conversion POE encapsulant for enhancing stability in back-contact silicon photovoltaic modules
,” published in
Solar Energy
. The research team comprised scientists from China’s
Jiangsu University of Science and Technology

title: Bomb attacks on solar plants in Colombia leave facilities offline - pv magazine Global
content:
After several years of relative calm following the 2016 peace agreement, Colombia has experienced a resurgence of armed guerrilla activity, alongside growing violence targeting critical infrastructure, including electricity generation and transmission facilities.
The country’s solar sector has also been affected, with Colombian renewable energy producer Evolti reporting a new attack involving explosives on its Delta 1 and Delta 2 solar farms in El Remolino, in the municipality of Taminango, in Colombia’s southwestern department of Nariño. The Nov. 23 attack follows an Oct. 29 attack on the Naos 3 solar plant in the same area. A spokesperson from Evolti told
pv magazine
that two of the three affected facilities remain offline and that one of its employees has been held captive since Oct. 3.
FOOTAGE OF THE EXPLOSION
https://www.pv-magazine-latam.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/WhatsApp-Video-2026-11-26-at-4.53.25-PM.mp4
According to the 2025 operations and market report by XM, the operator of Colombia’s National Interconnected System (SIN), the Delta 1 and Delta 2 solar plants each have a net effective capacity of 0.99 MW, while Naos 3 has a capacity of 0.96 MW. All three facilities, with a combined capacity of 2.94 MW, were connected to the Colombian grid in 2025.
“In addition to material damage, the attacks are affecting energy generation: Naos 3 and Delta 1 are out of operation, which reduces the energy we supply to the grid,” Evolti’s spokesperson explained to
pv magazine
. The company estimates that the combined output of its Naos and Delta solar complexes is equivalent to the electricity consumption of nearly 20,000 households. Its technical team is assessing the damage in coordination with the authorities; however, no estimate of the economic losses or a timeline for resuming operations has been provided thus far.
Although none of the attacks on the solar plants resulted in injuries, Evolti revealed that two of its employees were kidnapped on October 3. One has since been released and is with his family, while the other remains in captivity. Furthermore, both the company and its staff have received threats.
When asked by
pv magazine
about the potential involvement of guerrilla organizations, the company stated that it has no confirmation, though it does not rule out this hypothesis. Regarding the possible motives behind the attacks, Evolti points to both economic extortion and the use of violence against energy infrastructure as a means of exerting political pressure on the Colombian government.
“The attacks also put our team at risk, negatively impact employment and the opportunities these projects bring to local communities, and hinder the arrival of new investment in the region,” the company’s spokesperson stated. In an official release dated November 23, Evolti called on the national government to take immediate action to protect its workers and energy infrastructure, and announced that it has begun the process of filing a formal complaint with the Office of the Attorney General.
Founded in 2020 in Pasto, the capital of the Nariño department, Evolti is involved in the development, investment, construction, and operation of renewable energy projects. According to data provided to
pv magazine
, the company has 350 employees, operates in eight Colombian departments, and has an installed capacity of 40 MW, with a goal of reaching 100 MW by 2027. Since its inception, it has developed more than 30 photovoltaic farms and 120 solar projects in the country. In November 2025, the company announced a partnership with the energy retailer and generator BIA Energy to develop over 30 MW of photovoltaic capacity in the department of Valle del Cauca.
The attacks against Evolti occur within a context of rising violence targeting the Colombian electricity sector. On November 10, Celsia reported an attack on its 19.9 MW Amaime hydroelectric plant, located in Palmira, Valle del Cauca. On November 15, attacks were recorded against electrical transmission infrastructure in the department of Huila. Earlier that month, reports also emerged that Empresas Públicas de Medellín (EPM) had raised concerns with the Colombian Congress regarding threats and extortion demands linked to the Hidroituango hydroelectric project.
On November 24—one day after the latest attack on Evolti’s photovoltaic plants—a new incident involving the ISA Energía transmission network caused power supply interruptions across five departments: Cauca, Nariño, Putumayo, Caquetá, and Huila. The Ministry of Mines and Energy attributed the incident to an attack on electrical infrastructure and announced a special protection plan for electricity and gas facilities. As of Thursday, November 26, XM has confirmed that power supply restrictions persist in the five affected departments.

title: Terra Clove completes maiden voyage on ammonia fuel
content:
Terra Clove completes maiden voyage on ammonia fuel
Eastern Pacific Shipping continues on-water operations
Eastern Pacific Shipping’s new dual-fuel vessel – the Very Large Ammonia Carrier (VLAC) Terra Clove – has successfully utilised ammonia as fuel during her maiden voyage and “continues to operate successfully at sea”. The news follows the successful completion of ammonia-fueled trials, and subsequent delivery in October from the shipyard.
The Terra Clove was built by South Korea-based Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) and is powered by Everllence’s B&W 6G60ME-C10.5-LGIA two-stroke engine. The vessel can carry 93,000m³ of ammonia as cargo and can be propelled by ammonia or conventional marine fuel. Renewable ammonia fuel for trials and commercial operations is being supplied by South Korea-based LOTTE Fine Chemicals (LOTTE), and produced by China-based Envision Energy.

title: NYK unveils the ammonia-fueled medium gas carrier Izanami
content:
NYK unveils the ammonia-fueled medium gas carrier Izanami
Vessel launched in Japan, to be time chartered to Yara Clean Ammonia
NYK has named and unveiled its newly completed ammonia-fueled medium gas carrier at Japan Marine United Corporation’s Ariake Shipyard. In a world-first, the Izanami features ammonia-fueled engines for both main and auxiliary power. Launched in 2021 as a part of the NEDO Green Innovation Fund Project for next-generation vessels program, NYK, Nihon Shipyard, Japan Engine Corporation (2-stroke main engine), IHI Power Systems (4-stroke auxiliary engine), and recently ClassNK (safety accreditation for ammonia engine rooms) have now advanced the project from “development to the operational phase”, as the vessel prepares for commercial operations. The Izanami was bunkered with ammonia fuel via a ship-to-ship transfer in September, powering ocean trials.
The vessel will be time-chartered to Yara Clean Ammonia, following an agreement signed in 2025. NYK indicates that the time-charter period will be used to verify operational performance, safety considerations, and measurable GHG reductions under actual operating conditions. These insights will assist the development and operation of future ammonia-fueled vessels in NYK’s fleet.
The name “Izanami” derives from Izanami-no-Mikoto, a deity in Japanese mythology responsible for forming the islands of Japan. This name was chosen in the hope that the vessel will symbolize the dawn of a new era of next-generation energy beginning in Japan.
NYK has also developed the tugboat Sakigake, the world’s first commercially operated ammonia-fueled vessel, which has been in continuous operation since August 2024. Presented to the IMO in September 2026, Sakigake Captain Kawai explains that, although initial operations of the vessel came with many unknowns, real-world experience across a range of different operating profiles has helped build confidence amongst the crew. Similar to onboard the Izanami, potential exposure of the tugboat crew to ammonia fuel components was “designed out” during the retrofit process of the Sakigake, ensuring that risks do not have to be actively managed during operations.

ACME completes FID on Odisha project
760,00 tons per year, mixture of export and local demand
India-based ACME Group has completed FID on its second renewable ammonia project: a 760,000 tons per year plant in Gopalpur Industrial Park, Odisha, with a total investment of around $3.6 billion. Brookfield partnered with ACME in September 2026 as a marquee clean fuels investor with a commitment of up to $600 million, and thyssenkrupp Uhde has been announced as ACME’s green ammonia technology partner. ACME also indicates that the ammonia produced in Odisha has been pre-certified as RFNBO-compliant by CertifHy.
Expected to be commissioned by 2029, the joint ACME-IHI ammonia production project was launched in 2023. The pair plan to export 400,000 tons per year to Japan, backed by the recent awarding of CfD subsidies from the Japanese government. ACME indicates that CfD funding will cover 228,000 tons per year of this total over a 25-year period (starting September 2030), delivered to an IHI-led consortium at the future Tomakomai ammonia import hub in Hokkaido. The remaining 177,000 tons will be supported under Japan’s Long-Term Decarbonized Power Source Auction (LTDPA), likely for co-firing in coal power plants. The Odisha plant will also supply 370,000 tons of renewable ammonia per year to domestic fertiliser producers via SECI’s renewable ammonia auction round, including Paradeep Phosphates, Coromandel International, IFFCO, and Indorama India.
In 2023 ACME secured a loan from REC Limited (one of India’s largest green infrastructure financial firms) to fully finance the first phase of the Duqm renewable ammonia project in Oman, which earlier this year accepted delivery of electrolyser equipment from China.
The Final Investment Decision on our Odisha green ammonia project marks a critical milestone as we move from ambition to execution at scale. Building on the learnings from our Green Ammonia Duqm project in Oman, designed exclusively for the European RFNBO market, the Odisha project demonstrates India’s ability to produce competitive green molecules for diverse markets and end uses. The project is underpinned by long-term offtake commitments from customers in India, Japan and the European Union. We thank Brookfield for its confidence in the project as a marquee investor. Together, we are building a platform to help decarbonise hard-to-abate industries and strengthen energy security in India and globally.
Manoj Kumar Upadhyay, Chairman ACME Group, in his organisation’s official press release, 18 Nov 2026
We are pleased to partner with Acme’s green molecule business. With our commitment of US$600 million, coupled with Acme’s own invested capital, we believe the business is well positioned to deliver on over 1.5 mtpa of green molecule projects in the near to medium term, backed by long term offtake from strong global counterparties. The Odisha project is an important part of that business plan and we look forward to see the project advancing to the next stage of execution.
Murzash Manekshana, Head of Asset Management in India, Energy, Brookfield, in ACME’s official press release, 18 Nov 2026

title: 科学网-多所高校向师生提供免费词元：额度有高低，路径各不同
content:
多所高校向师生提供免费词元：额度有高低，路径各不同
又有一所高校向师生提供免费词元（Token）。
2026年11月27日，复旦大学宣布，面向全校师生免费开放大模型API服务，每人每周初始配额为1亿Token。在此之前，上海已有多所高校向师生开放了词元额度。同济大学人工智能服务平台为每位师生提供专属API Key，平台上线后每周1000积分(折合约1亿词元)。华东师范大学走的是“免申请直发”路线，基础词元配额直接发放至学校AI平台个人账户，科研竞赛项目可再申请专项大额额度。沪上高校中额度最高的是上海交通大学，“交我算”平台提供的词元额度为每周10亿。值得注意的是，每所高校开放API（ Application Programming Interface，意为应用程序编程接口）服务的场景和计费口径不尽相同，因此不能单看词元额度多少。
放眼全国，中国科学技术大学的“词元计划”面向全体在校师生每人每天1亿词元免费额度，次日清零重置，可调用DeepSeek、GLM、千问等多个主流模型。北京大学则选择了更聚焦的路径，与企业合作为师生免费提供一年Qoder编程智能体服务，每个账号每月3000 Credits（积分），达到限额后可申请追加，但闲置账号会被回收。清华大学的做法是发放“算力券”：全体在校师生可领取1000元基础算力额度，针对算力需求更高的师生，审核通过后，每人还可额外申领2000元算力加油包。
单从市价看，1亿词元的账面价值并不惊人，据AI从业者的估算，约合25元人民币。对于习惯调用商业API的用户而言，这不过是一次中等规模实验的成本。
但高校发放词元的逻辑，从来不是“发钱”。复旦在公告中明确强调，将提供稳定、安全、可靠的服务，校内词元服务可减少数据向外部公有云外流，师生未发表的实验数据、核心专利草稿及敏感文件全程在校内网闭环流转，“从物理层和网络层降低敏感信息泄露风险”，这是公有云API无法提供的安全底线。
更重要的是“不限请求次数”带来的使用心理变化，当额度按周重置、请求次数不设上限，师生在科研对话、代码调试、文献梳理时便不必反复计算“这次调用划不划算”。一位使用校内词元的学生形容，这就像从“按流量计费”换成了“包周套餐”，自己也敢让模型多跑几轮，因为试错成本被学校兜住了。
“发词元”正在成为2026年中国高校的一个标志性动作，额度有高低，路径各不同，但方向一致：把算力从稀缺商品变成校园基础设施，让AI真正进入日常教学与科研的“毛细血管”。

title: 科学网-新型复合凝胶为糖尿病难愈创面修复提供新方案
content:
新型复合凝胶为糖尿病难愈创面修复提供新方案
11月27日，记者从陆军军医大学西南医院获悉，该院内分泌科隆敏教授团队联合深圳大学许太林教授、陆军特色医学中心范娅涵主任团队，通过研发抗氧化复合血小板凝胶，破解传统血小板凝胶治疗糖尿病伤口效果不理想的难题。相关成果以《富血小板血浆-TPGN复合凝胶依托核因子E2相关蛋白通路清除活性氧，加快糖尿病创面再上皮化》为题发表在国际知名期刊《先进科学》上，为糖尿病慢性伤口临床治疗提供全新思路。
“糖尿病慢性创面是糖尿病最为棘手的并发症之一。创面长期处于高糖微环境中，会持续产生大量活性氧，阻碍皮肤修复细胞迁移、扰乱胶原蛋白合成，最终导致创面迁延不愈。”第一作者、西南医院内分泌科博士后蔺洁茹介绍，血小板凝胶是临床常用的创面修复材料，但创面内过量的活性氧会破坏修复生长因子活性，导致其临床疗效受限。如何突破这一治疗困境、提升糖尿病慢性创面愈合效率，是临床亟待攻克的现实难题。
“针对这一临床痛点，我们将成熟的血小板凝胶技术与活性氧响应型纳米材料有机结合，研发出这款复合修复凝胶。”隆敏表示，研究团队以葡萄糖为基础骨架，制备出可高效清除活性氧的纳米微粒；随后将纳米微粒与富血小板血浆混合，通过三通连接装置喷涂于创面即可原位形成凝胶，可适配各类形态不规则的创面。
研究团队通过细胞水平、动物模型及基因调控层面的系列实验，逐层验证凝胶的创面修复效能。细胞实验结果显示，该复合凝胶既可清除细胞内过量活性氧、保护修复生长因子活性，助力皮肤细胞完成迁移修复；还能激活机体核因子E2相关蛋白（NRF2）抗氧化调控机制，调控下游蛋白发挥防护与修复作用。
动物实验结果表明，使用该凝胶后，糖尿病创面愈合速度显著加快，皮肤再生质量、胶原沉积及肉芽组织生长状态均得到明显改善。基因干预实验证实，若阻断NRF2抗氧化调控机制，凝胶的修复效应会显著减弱，进一步印证了该机制的核心作用。
“通过系列实验验证，我们明确这款复合凝胶可实现氧化损伤清除、内源性抗氧化激活、创面再生修复三重效应，突破了传统修复材料在糖尿病创面高氧化微环境下疗效不足的瓶颈，为糖尿病慢性创面临床治疗提供了全新路径。”隆敏说。
下一步，研究团队将持续探索新型复合凝胶，优化材料性能与配方参数，稳步推进成果转化进程，力争早日应用于临床，为饱受慢性创面困扰的糖尿病患者带来愈合新希望。

兰州大学发布严正声明
关于我校同等学力申请硕士学位招生的严正声明
近期部分机构或个人，以“兰州大学”、“兰大”、“兰州大学某机构”或“兰州大学硕士研究生”的名义，建立招生网站或新媒体账号，违规发布同等学力申请硕士虚假招生宣传信息。为维护学校办学声誉，规范我校同等学力申请硕士学位招生秩序，切实保障广大学员合法权益，现就招生相关事宜严正声明如下：
一、我校从未以任何形式委托任何教育培训机构或个人面向社会进行同等学力申请硕士学位招生宣传与收费，从未设立所谓任何与兰州大学同等学力申请硕士学位相关的机构。我校招生信息以学校官网、官方新媒体平台等发布的内容为准。
二、我校同等学力申请硕士学位面向社会公开招生，请在兰州大学网络与继续教育学院、兰州大学培训中心官网或相关学院官网的招生通知查看相关信息，符合条件的人员均可直接报名，各类收费均严格按照学校规定的收费标准收取，并出具兰州大学正式票据。严禁将学费交由任何机构、个人或非授权单位代收，由此产生的任何后果，我校概不负责。
三、我校同等学力申请硕士学位项目严格规范办学。请广大学员勿相信“交费包过”“不用上课”“不用考试”“1.5年学制”“毕业双证”等虚假宣传，避免上当受骗。
四、对一切未经我校同意，以“兰州大学”名义进行非法招生宣传等活动的任何机构或个人，学校保留依法追究其责任的权利。

content:
哈尔滨工程大学深海机器人研究院成立
中新网哈尔滨11月27日电 (史轶夫 胡莹洁)11月27日，哈尔滨工程大学深海机器人研究院成立大会在哈尔滨举行。成立仪式上，发布了全球首个海洋通用基座大模型“沧穹 CEORION”。
哈尔滨工程大学深海机器人研究院成立大会在哈尔滨举行。哈工程供图
哈尔滨工程大学是“三海一核”领域重要的科学研究和人才培养基地，建有智能海洋航行器技术全国重点实验室、水声技术全国重点实验室等一批高水平科研平台。
深海机器人研究院由哈尔滨工程大学与世航智能科技股份有限公司联合共建，聚焦深海机器人、新概念海洋机器人等前沿方向，打造集基础研究探索、关键技术攻关、产品技术创新、成果转化、人才培养、行业服务于一体的高水平创新载体。
成立仪式上，发布了全球首个海洋通用基座大模型“沧穹 CEORION”。　郭健楠 摄
成立仪式上，发布了全球首个海洋通用基座大模型“沧穹 CEORION”。该模型基于语言-世界-动作模型统一架构，动态融合视觉、声学、压力、流体、姿态等多维度传感数据，搭建端到端统一神经网络，能够实现语义理解、环境建模和动作生成的融合，并且实现水下环境感知、任务研判、路径规划、自主作业、应急处置等全流程自主闭环以及指数级泛化的通用智能能力。这是中国企业在海洋通用人工智能领域实现的原始性突破。
未来，哈尔滨工程大学与世航智能科技股份有限公司将优势互补、协同创新，依托深海机器人研究院，联合申报国家级创新平台，联合制定国家及行业标准，联合承担国家及省市重大项目，联合培养高端人才，共同打造一支高水平科教融合团队，推进深海机器人技术产业化应用落地，推动深海机器人产教深度融合，以一体推进教育科技人才发展助推深海智能装备向智向新，为中国深海事业高质量发展贡献更大力量。(完)

title: 科学网-“感到震惊”，顶尖名校宣布暂停数学博士招生
content:
“感到震惊”，顶尖名校宣布暂停数学博士招生
文｜《中国科学报》记者孙滔
原定12月15日截止的博士申请，还没到截止日就作废了。
近日，美国常春藤名校达特茅斯学院宣布，数学博士项目将暂停2027—2028学年新生招生。这个项目每年通常招收7至9人。已经递交的申请材料和推荐信，校方不再审阅。
据《达特茅斯报》报道，校方给出的理由是，文理学院正在对数学系开展院系评估。但这项评估何时结束，博士招生何时恢复，校方均未给出明确答案。
这并不是美国大学第一次暂停数学博士招生。今年早些时候，乔治·华盛顿大学也曾暂停数学博士项目一个招生周期。不同大学接连作出类似决定，难免让人追问：美国大学的数学博士培养正在发生什么变化？
一位不愿具名的达特茅斯数学系教授在接受《中国科学报》采访时表示，暂停数学博士招生，首先与美国联邦政府对理论研究支持力度下降，以及大学管理层调整学科发展战略和投资方向有关。
图源：达特茅斯学院
“此前没有任何迹象”
据《达特茅斯报》报道，11月9日，达特茅斯举行全体教师大会。数学教授Peter Winkler在会上透露，数学系教师此前11月6日才获知这个决定。
校方公开给出的理由是：在文理学院对数学系开展院系评估期间，暂停2027—2028学年数学博士项目招生，以便重新审视研究生教育资源的配置。
会上，教师们对这一决定表达了担忧。
第二天，数学系主任Dimitrios Giannakis给研究生们发了一封邮件。他说，教师们正在与学院管理层沟通，希望“找到一条可行的出路”，最终“恢复博士项目招生”。
但他并不乐观：“我不认为暂停招生的决定会被撤销，但我希望至少能够开展建设性对话，并取得一些可以落实的成果。”
在读博士生感受到的，则是随之而来的不确定性和不稳定感。
三年级博士生Jacob Lehmann Duke说：“我们所有人都感到震惊。此前没有任何迹象表明会发生这样的事。”
值得注意的是，暂停招生并不意味着停办。达特茅斯研究生院院长Carrie Colla向在读博士生保证，现有学生的学籍、津贴、保险和五年资助承诺均不受影响，学校将支持他们完成学业。
科学作家Susan D’Agostino曾在达特茅斯获得数学博士学位。对于母校暂停招生，她深感遗憾。她在美国高等教育媒体Inside Higher Ed上撰文说，人工智能（AI）时代，数学博士教育不应该只培养做数学研究的人，还应该培养能够理解数学、讲授数学和传播数学的人。达特茅斯的小规模博士项目恰恰体现了这种教育理念。
一个颇具历史意味的细节是，达特茅斯被认为是AI这一学科的发源地。1955年，几位科学家在筹备一场研讨会时，首次使用了“人工智能”这一术语。1956年夏天，研讨会在达特茅斯举行，后来被视为AI学科诞生的标志。70年后，当AI开始改变数学研究的方式，它的“命名地”却暂停了数学博士招生。
达特茅斯的这一决定背后，或许有着多重原因。
前述达特茅斯数学系教授告诉《中国科学报》，学校管理层目前的战略重点与联邦政府的优先发展方向基本一致，包括多学科交叉、AI及其在不同学科中的应用。
更值得关注的是，这位教授认为，AI的发展正在冲击传统数学博士培养模式。
他特别提到，随着AI在数学研究中的能力不断增强，部分数学突破的速度甚至可能超过人类数学家的理解和验证能力。在他看来，这对以人类独立提出问题、完成证明并接受学术训练为核心的传统数学博士培养模式构成了巨大挑战。
经费是该教授提到的另一个重要因素。据他估算，达特茅斯培养一名数学博士，五年的总投入至少需要50万美元。不过，这一数字的具体计算口径还需要进一步说明。
与此同时，研究生工会通过集体谈判争取更高的津贴和福利，也意味着大学需要承担更长期、更稳定的博士培养支出。这也是评估博士培养成本时值得关注的因素。
受访教授认为，在大学管理者看来，传统数学博士项目不仅需要重新审视培养模式和投入方式，也需要回答一个现实问题：在AI快速发展的背景下，学校为什么还需要继续维持这样的博士培养项目？
美国大学正在调整博士招生，已经不是孤立事件。
美国大学协会（AAU）2026年7月公布的一项调查显示，55所研究型大学2026年秋季博士项目录取人数比上一年下降了15%。
今年早些时候，乔治·华盛顿大学宣布2026—2027学年暂停五个博士项目的招生，数学博士项目就在其中。
不过，两所大学的情况并不完全一样。乔治·华盛顿大学暂停招生与博士生资助跟财政压力直接相关，目的是限制新的资助承诺，确保兑现对在读博士生的资助；而达特茅斯目前公开的解释则是数学系院系评估。
目前，乔治·华盛顿大学数学系官网已经公布，将在2027年秋季招生周期重新提供全额资助的博士生名额。
前述达特茅斯教授认为，美国高校研究生培养正在经历一场结构性调整。
“过去是研究生培养的‘工厂时代’，如今美国不少名校的博士项目都在缩编，背后是政府科研资金投入不足，以及高校对基础研究人才培养投入的减少。”

title: 科学网-毒药变良药，“砒霜疗法”成抗癌国际方案
content:
毒药变良药，“砒霜疗法”成抗癌国际方案
近日，中国科学院院士陈竺与法国医学家安妮·德尚、戴宇阁共同获得2026年度邵逸夫生命科学与医学奖。他们三人共同阐释了急性早幼粒细胞白血病（APL）在分子与细胞层面的致病基础，开创了协同靶向治疗方案，使这种疾病转变为治愈率最高的癌症之一，治愈率超过90%。这一协同靶向治疗方案的核心药物之一，是以砒霜主要成分三氧化二砷为基础的砷剂。它与全反式维甲酸联用治疗APL的方案，在中国常被通俗地称为“砒霜疗法”。
继青蒿素之后，“砒霜疗法”从中国走向全球，成为被国际指南采纳的标准治疗方案。两者走通了高度相似的创新之路，均扎根于本土传统医药智慧，以现代科学范式拆解机理、严格循证，最终把古老线索转化成能够拯救无数生命的全球医学方案。
发现“以毒攻毒”方案
APL曾是最凶险的白血病亚型，在“砒霜疗法”诞生之前，化疗是主流治疗手段，但其副作用大，复发率高，患者长期生存希望渺茫。北京大学人民医院主任医师张晓辉表示，在APL治疗方面，中国人走到了世界前列，创造了“维甲酸+砷剂”治疗模式，让绝大多数患者完全可以达到正常人的生活水平。
这份改写癌症诊疗史的成果，既涵盖了传统“以毒攻毒”的朴素经验，也凝结了几代科学家接续攻关、中西思路交融、跨国科研协作的严谨求索。
上世纪70年代，黑龙江省哈尔滨医科大学附属第一医院医生张亭栋听说大庆市林甸县一个卫生院用毒药治癌症。他带队前往查访，发现老中医用的方子中有三味剧毒药物：砒霜、轻粉、蟾酥。他根据实践逐步改造方子以降低毒性，并发现真正产生疗效的是其中的砒霜，主要成分是三氧化二砷。
1973年，张亭栋等人在《黑龙江医药》发表小样本临床观察，报道了通过剂量摸索在安全和效果间寻找最优解的实践，发现用6毫克砷剂注射液取得了很好临床效果。
北京大学终身讲席教授饶毅曾在《中药的科学研究丰碑》中阐述，三氧化二砷源于观察、验证和改进乡村中医的实践。他们的研究显示，青蒿素和三氧化二砷都是以现代科学的方法所获得，遵循科学的标准所确立其效果。
阐明治疗分子机理
在上海，“驯化”肿瘤细胞的工作也在持续开展。1988年，上海瑞金医院医生王振义课题组在美国《血液》杂志发表论文，总结用全反式维甲酸治疗24例APL病人的经验。几年后，王振义的学生陈竺、陈赛娟夫妇从法国归来，注意到张亭栋用砷剂治疗APL的研究。他们利用分子生物学手段解析了三氧化二砷治疗APL的分子机制，揭示砷剂在诱导关键基因表达、降解融合蛋白、诱导APL白血病细胞凋亡等方面的详细机制。
王振义、陈竺团队与张亭栋团队开展合作，在全面系统研究静脉注射砷剂的药代动力学和毒理学的基础上，将砷剂用于对维甲酸耐药的患者，取得了良好疗效，并在世界上首先阐明三氧化二砷治疗白血病的细胞和分子机理。
随着治疗的推进，他们发现单独使用砷剂长期治疗后，部分患者也会出现耐药性。2000年以来，陈竺、陈赛娟等通过持续深入的多中心、前瞻性、规范的大组临床研究，发现维甲酸和砷剂合用的方案可使90%以上的APL获得治愈，证明了此方案的长期安全性，并明确了两种药物通过不同机制靶向作用于APL的致癌蛋白。
这些成果使APL治疗成为国际上癌症协同靶向治疗的成功范例，国际血液学界将这套“维甲酸+砷剂”联合方案称为“上海方案”。“‘青蒿截疟’‘砒霜攻毒’的药理机制与临床疗效获得了全球学界的重复验证与广泛认可。”国家药品监督管理局原副局长、四川省中医药科学院原院长赵军宁表示，尽管传统药物与现代药物在物质来源、理论依据与研发路径上存在差异，但在概念内涵上并没有本质差异。事实上，在抗肿瘤药、抗感染药等领域，有百分之六七十的小分子药物来自天然产物。在传统中医长期人用经验和临床疗效确认的基础上，如果能够进一步用现代科学解读中医药作用机理，建立一套可对话、可验证、可传播的现代学术语言，就能经受全世界科学界的重复验证。
解读中药千年“黑箱”
“陈竺院士的系统解析，是在临床疗效确实的前提下推进的。这种有明确目标的探索方式，相较于没有临床或传统经验支撑的化合物筛选，有更高成功率。陈竺院士团队的工作为肿瘤协同靶向治疗提供了具有里程碑意义的成功范例。”赵军宁说，过去半个世纪，国际上无论是表型药物发现，还是靶点药物发现，时间和经济成本都很高。新药研发的高投入高失败率提示，现有药物研发将复杂人体系统简化为可研究模型，再回归到复杂人体系统验证的路径，存在转化上的巨大鸿沟，这也是原创新药研发成功往往需要耗费十年、数十亿美元的原因之一。
当前的药物研发数据也证实了这一点：动物实验有效药物进入临床试验、最终实现上市的几率不到10%。相较而言，中医药多年来的临床实践人用经验是特点和优势所在。
赵军宁认为，药物有效性的本质是复杂的、体系化的整体治疗效应，而非单一靶点的孤立作用，这恰为中医药复方的现代开发留出空间，从中医药中提炼原创医疗方案潜力巨大。
“无论是青蒿素还是砷剂，它们都找到了单一成分进行逆向解析，推动中医药成功走向国际。这条技术路线是可以走通的。”赵军宁表示，如何认识中药复方的原理和科学规律，是需要持续深入探索的问题。
当前，面向复杂慢病研发具备多靶向系统性调节和干预功能的药物，已成为全球新药研发新风向标。其涉及多组分协同、药物相互作用，机理研究的复杂程度将呈指数倍增加。“随着技术手段不断进步、科学认识日益加深，把中医药疗效优势说明白、讲清楚的机遇已成为可及现实，前景光明。”赵军宁解释，方剂之效不等于成分加和，配伍产生了单味药不具备的“新质”。例如，近20年来的研究发现，中药及其复方里的有效物质，很多并不单独以游离单体的形式起效，而是以多成分自组装成纳米颗粒，发挥组合药理作用。方剂纳米体，作为介于方剂整体与单体化学成分之间的纳米聚集体，具有可表征的多层次结构与相态特征，是承载复方多成分协同药效的重要物质形式。借助方剂纳米体，研究人员可在介观尺度重新认识中药复方的固有物质组织方式与协同逻辑，以可验证、可理解的现代科学语言阐释中医药。
“技术的新突破将加深人类对中医药的理解，让中药千年‘黑箱’被读懂、被复现、被更好利用。”赵军宁说，我国在中药监管方面已实现从传统经验管理、简单行政执法到科学监管，再到智慧监管的转变。近期，国家药品监督管理局专门召开了中药监管工作座谈会，提出将进一步加大中药领域政策支持力度，优化监管模式和评价方法，完善指导原则体系，巩固拓展中药创新研发，推动名方验方、医疗机构中药制剂等向新药转化，拓宽天然药物研发路径，扎实推进中药传承创新发展。

新一代人工智能国家科技重大专项项目申报指南发布
关于发布新一代人工智能国家科技重大专项2027年度第一批公开项目申报指南的通知
为加快实施新一代人工智能国家科技重大专项（以下简称“重大专项”），根据重大专项阶段性实施计划部署，现将2027年度第一批公开项目申报指南予以公布。请按照指南要求组织项目申报工作，有关事项通知如下。
一、项目组织申报工作流程
1.申报单位根据指南支持方向的研究内容，以项目为单元整体申报。申报项目须覆盖相应指南方向的全部考核指标；项目设1名负责人，每个课题设1名负责人，项目负责人可担任其中1个课题的负责人。项目下设课题数一般不超过5个，项目参与单位总数一般不超过10家，具体要求以指南为准。
2.整合优势创新团队，并积极吸纳青年科研人员和女性科研人员参与项目研发，聚焦指南任务，集中力量，联合攻关。鼓励有能力的青年科研人员和女性科研人员作为项目（课题）负责人领衔担纲承担任务。
3.项目申报评审具体工作流程如下：
项目申报单位根据指南相关申报要求，通过国家科技管理信息系统公共服务平台（http：//service.most.gov.cn，以下简称“国科管系统”）填写并提交项目申报书。
项目的牵头单位应与所有参与单位签署联合申报协议，明确各单位任务分工、经费分配、知识产权归属等；项目（课题）负责人应在联合申报协议上签字，协议签署时间应明确体现。项目牵头申报单位、课题申报单位、所有参与单位、项目负责人及课题负责人须签署诚信承诺书，并严格遵守承诺。项目牵头申报单位及所有参与单位要落实《关于进一步加强科研诚信建设的若干意见》《关于进一步弘扬科学家精神加强作风和学风建设的意见》要求，加强对申报材料审核把关，杜绝夸大不实，严禁弄虚作假。
新一代人工智能国家科技重大专项专项办公室（以下简称“专项办”）在受理项目申报后，组织形式审查，并组织答辩评审。申报项目的负责人进行报告答辩，根据专家评议情况择优立项。项目立项后建立动态调整机制，结合过程管理开展关键节点考核评估，根据评估结果确定后续支持方式。
二、组织申报的推荐单位
1.国务院有关部门科技主管司局；
2.各省、自治区、直辖市、计划单列市及新疆生产建设兵团科技主管部门；
3.原工业部门转制成立的行业协会；
4.纳入科技部试点范围并且评估结果为A类的产业技术创新战略联盟，以及纳入科技部、财政部开展的科技服务业创新发展行业试点联盟；
5.港澳科研单位牵头申报的项目，分别由香港创新科技署、澳门科学技术发展基金按要求组织推荐。
各推荐单位应在本单位职能和业务范围内推荐，并对所推荐项目的真实性等负责。
三、申报资格要求
1.项目牵头申报单位和参与单位应为中国大陆境内注册的具有独立法人资格的科研院所、高等学校和企业等单位，或内地与香港、内地与澳门科技合作委员会协商确定的港澳单位（附件），注册时间为2026年1月30日前，有较强的科技研发能力和条件，运行管理规范。国家机关不得牵头或参与申报。
项目申报单位、参与单位以及项目团队成员诚信状况良好，无在惩戒执行期内的科研严重失信行为记录和相关社会领域信用“黑名单”记录。
2.项目（课题）负责人须具有高级职称或博士学位，1966年12月30日以后出生，每年用于项目的工作时间不得少于6个月。
3.项目（课题）负责人原则上应为该项目（课题）主体研究思路的提出者和实际主持研究的科技人员。中央和地方各级国家机关的公务人员（包括行使科技计划管理职能的其他人员）不得申报项目（课题）。
4.申报人在本专项本次申报中作为项目（课题）负责人仅限申报1项。项目（课题）负责人每年用于本项目的工作时间不得少于6个月。
5.已有在研或同期申报的国家科技重大专项、国家重点研发计划重点专项项目（课题）负责人不得作为项目（课题）负责人牵头申报本专项项目。
6.项目（课题）负责人、项目骨干的申报项目（课题）和国家科技重大专项、国家重点研发计划在研项目（课题）总数不得超过2个。
7.国家科技重大专项、国家重点研发计划在研项目（课题）负责人及骨干不得因申报新项目（课题）而退出目前承担的项目；退出项目研发团队后，在原项目执行期内原则上不得牵头或参与申报本重大专项。
8.中央财政专项资金预算不超过400万元的“政府间国际科技创新合作”重点专项项目和“战略性科技创新合作”重点专项，不在限项范围内。
9.按照《科技部办公厅财政部办公厅自然科学基金委办公室关于进一步加强统筹国家科技计划项目立项管理工作的通知》（国科办资〔2022〕107号）有关限项要求，重大专项的项目（课题）负责人，需与国家自然科学基金重大项目（限项目负责人和课题负责人）、基础科学中心项目（限学术带头人和骨干成员）、国家重大科研仪器研制项目（限部门推荐项目的项目负责人和具有高级职称的主要参与者）实施联合限项，科研人员同期申报和在研的项目（课题）数原则上不得超过2项。
10.计划任务书执行期（包括延期后的执行期）到2026年12月30日及之前的在研项目（含任务或课题）不在限项范围内。
11.如无特殊说明，本指南所称国家科技重大专项包含科技创新2030-重大项目、重大专项接续项目和面向2035的重大项目等。具体规定参照《科技部办公厅财政部办公厅自然科学基金委办公室关于进一步加强统筹国家科技计划项目立项管理工作的通知》（国科办资〔2022〕107号）。
12.参与本重大专项实施方案、阶段性实施计划或本年度项目指南编制的专家，不能申报项目（课题）。
13.受聘于内地单位的外籍科学家及港澳台地区科学家可作为项目（课题）负责人，全职受聘人员须由内地聘用单位提供全职聘用的有效材料，非全职受聘人员须由双方单位同时提供聘用的有效材料，并作为项目申报材料一并提交。
14.申报项目受理后，原则上不能更改申报单位和负责人。
15.申报项目如有50万及以上的设备购置，申报单位须如实提交本单位现有同类设备存量清单，列明设备型号、数量、在用状态、采购日期等相关信息，并加盖单位公章，作为设备购置必要性审核的重要依据。
16.项目申报单位编制项目预算时，提供其他来源资金的企业应当提供近三年经审计后的财务报表及其他来源资金出资方的出资承诺，原则上应以货币资金作为资金来源，不得使用本项目外中央及地方财政项目资金或中央及地方财政项目资金形成的资产作为资金来源。
17.根据《科技伦理审查办法（试行）》（国科发监〔2023〕167号）等有关管理办法要求，凡涉及科技伦理问题的申报项目，均应按规定开展科技伦理审查，并提交相关审查材料。
18.项目的具体申报要求，详见项目申报指南（附件），有特殊规定的，从其规定。
各申报单位在正式提交项目申报书前可利用国科管系统查询相关科研人员承担国家科技项目情况，避免重复申报。
四、具体申报方式
1.网上填报。请各申报单位按要求通过国科管系统进行网上填报。专项办将以网上填报的申报书作为后续形式审查、项目评审和组织论证的依据。申报材料中所需的附件材料，全部以电子扫描件上传。项目申报单位网上填报项目申报书的受理时间为：2026年12月4日10:00至2026年12月27日12:00。
2.组织推荐。申报书须经相关单位推荐。各推荐单位应加强对所推荐的项目申报材料的审核把关，于2027年1月4日16:00前通过国科管系统逐项确认推荐项目，并将加盖推荐单位公章的推荐函以电子扫描件上传。
每个项目只能通过单个推荐单位申报，不得多头申报和重复申报。
3.技术咨询电话及邮箱：
